#8924. The Science of “Extreme” Exercise During Pregnancy

The author attended the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto to hear directly from Margie Davenport and Michelle Mottola, key researchers shaping the upcoming 2027 International Olympic Committee guidelines. The resulting piece analyzes their latest clinical and survey data on pregnant athletes engaging in heavy weightlifting, high-intensity intervals, endurance sports, and rock climbing.

Back in 2019, I wrote about a new set of guidelines for exercise during pregnancy. These guidelines were revolutionary—up to a point. Advice from doctors at the time was often extremely conservative, like never letting your heart rate exceed 140 beats per minute. But solid evidence now suggested that consistent moderate exercise—at least 150 minutes spread over at least three days per week—was not just safe for most pregnant women but was actually beneficial for both mother and fetus, dramatically lowering the risk of conditions such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and depression.

Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more!

Beyond that threshold, though, the deadlines dared not tread. Moderate exercise? Sure. Lifting heavy weights, or running marathons, or going rock climbing? That’s a trickier question, because no scientist wants to send a pregnant person out to do something that could potentially harm her or her baby. But ignoring it doesn’t make sense, because many female athletes do continue participating in their sports while pregnant, regardless of what the guidelines say. And those who stop or dramatically reduce their activity may suffer declines in both physical and mental health.

It’s important, then, to understand what the evidence says about the risks and benefits of more extreme forms of exercise. In 2018, the answer was “not much.” But in the years since then, there has been a steady flow of research on pregnant athletes doing hard things. In fact, the International Olympic Committee is planning to release a new and dramatically revised set of guidelines for pregnant athletes in 2027.

At the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto last week, I had a chance to hear two key authors of both the old and new guidelines—Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University—speak about their research. They couldn’t yet reveal what’s in the new guidelines, but they did share some of the key research that informs them. Here are some highlights from the extreme frontiers of exercise and pregnancy.

Any sort of heavy lifting is frowned upon during pregnancy, and particularly lifting while lying on your back, which could compress key blood vessels. But this advice, Davenport points out, is based on expert opinion and workplace studies, where heavy lifting is different from lifting in the gym where you control load and recovery.

To start, she and her colleagues surveyed 679 recreational weightlifters and CrossFit athletes who were pregnant and habitually lifted at least 80 percent of their one-rep max. Those who continued heavy lifting had a 51 percent reduction in complications compared to those who obeyed the guidelines and dialed back their training. They were also roughly half as likely as normal to report postpartum depression after delivery.

Of course, survey studies have limitations: maybe complications caused people to stop lifting rather than the other way around, for example. But those initial positive results paved the way for bringing 10 pregnant women into the lab and having them do squats, bench press, and deadlift for 10 reps at up to 90 percent of 10-rep max. They monitored maternal and fetal heart rate, umbilical blood pressure, glucose and lactate levels, and various other health markers, and compared the results to those of ten non-pregnant controls; there were no causes for concern.

A heart-rate limit of 140 is outdated. Still, the 2019 guidelines remain cautious. “Vigorous” exercise, they suggest, should top out at around 169 beats per minute for women 29 and younger, and 162 beats per minute for those 30 and older.

In a 2023 study, Davenport and her colleagues put that ceiling to the test. They had 15 volunteers, at an average of 27 weeks pregnant, do either a 30-minute moderate bike ride or 10 x 1:00 intervals at above 90 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate. The women ended up reaching a peak of 96 percent on average during the intervals, with some getting as high as 105 percent of max. (This isn’t Spinal Tap: the standard estimate of max heart rate, 220 minus age, was clearly off for these women.)

Once again, the researchers took a bunch of measures of fetal and maternal physiological responses. There were no relevant differences between the moderate and intense exercise sessions.

This was another survey study: 331 women who, on average, were 33.2 years old and had completed 2.1 pregnancies. All had engaged in exercise bouts lasting at least an hour during their pregnancies; 80 percent had continued long-duration exercise throughout their pregnancies, but in most cases had gradually decreased overall training as the pregnancy progressed.

Davenport and her colleagues divided the respondents into two subgroups: those who continued to do at least 300 minutes of exercise per week during their third trimester, and those who were below that threshold. Those in the high exercise group had a lower risk of complications during delivery, but a higher risk of diastasis recti—a separation of the stomach muscles—after delivery.

The overall conclusion was that long-duration exercise well above guideline recommendations “appears to be well tolerated” by people who are already used to that level of training.

Here’s where things get interesting, because it’s hard to wave away the hypothetical dangers of a hard fall. But do these risks justify telling people not to climb?

Davenport has led a couple of studies exploring this issue. One involved interviewing 11 elite climbers who continued to train or compete during pregnancy about their perspectives on risk. Climbing, one of the climbers said, was actually safer than walking down the street: “I’m less likely to fall because I’ve got three points of contact on, compared to one when I’m walking… So I feel like I’m more likely to trip over something in the dark on the street than falling while climbing up a climbing wall.”

The second study surveyed nearly 700 climbers who had climbed through pregnancy, logging a cumulative total of 64,000 hours of climbing and suffering 155 self-diagnosed “hard falls.” Here there were two adverse events (one vaginal bleeding, the other undeclared), but both births were healthy. Climbing isn’t without risks, Davenport says, but the findings suggest the risks are lower than previously thought. Of note, 96 percent of respondents were “happy” or “very happy” they had continued to climb.

There’s more—Davenport has also studied contact sports like soccer, for example—but you get the picture. Some of these activities clearly involve theoretical risks, but those theoretical risks need to be balanced against the measurable mental and physical benefits of continuing to train and the risks of stopping. One of the best predictors of post-pregnancy injury, for example, is having reduced your training by more than 50 percent during pregnancy.

The focus of the upcoming IOC guidelines will be “athlete-centered decision-making”—not an ironclad set of rules about who can do which types of exercise when, but a framework about how to weigh the pros and cons in different contexts. It’s an important update, because it recognizes what’s already happening in the real world. “Our current public health guidance is fantastic and sets our baseline,” Davenport says. “But most athletes—well, all athletes—are going to vastly exceed current recommendations.”

#8923. How to Strengthen Your Arms and Wrists With Upward Plank Variations

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Upward Plank Pose variations first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

What direction do you face when you practice yoga? Probably whichever way your usual practice space dictates. But the old yogis were very clear that we should face either east or north when practicing, per the classical yoga text the Gheranda Samhita 5.48. Why?

Yoga scholar Alain Danielou writes that the four cardinal and four intermediate points of the compass have special significance. The thunderbolt-wielding Indra, lord of all the protectors and prototype of courage and power in Hindu mythology, guards the east.

By facing in a certain direction when we practice, we acknowledge and draw on energetic properties for support and inspiration. So again, why east and north? East is the quarter of the rising sun, which Hindus revere as the “breath of creatures” or the source of all earthly life.

The sun represents the embodied Self, its dawn the emergence of the “light” of spiritual self-awareness and insight. North is the quarter of the pole star, called dhruva (pronounced DREW-vah) in Sanskrit, meaning “fixed, eternal.” Its constancy amid the ever-wheeling night sky is considered the embodiment of willpower, certainly a quality all serious yogis covet. In India too, north is the realm of the majestic Himalayas, where Hindu tradition places the mythic mountain Meru, thought of as the “navel” of the earth as well as the bridge to the celestial world of the gods and goddesses.

What compass directions would you assign to the back and front of your body? According to the yogis, your back body is the west, your front body the east. In Sanskrit, paschima means both “back” and “west,” while purva means both “front” and “east.” So this terminology gives us the names of two common and related poses: Paschimottanasana (Intense Stretch of the West Pose or, more commonly, Seated Forward Bend), which stretches your back body, and Purvottanasana (Intense Stretch of the East or Upward Plank Pose)—pictured here—a slight backbend and front-body stretch that provides a nice counterpose to its western opposite.

Purvottanasana stretches you all the way from your ankles through the thighs, groins, and belly, up to the shoulders and throat. It also strengthens your wrists and the muscles on the backs of the upper arms (triceps) and firms the buttocks—which, if you believe popular media claims, is a primary benefit of yoga. It will also help improve your sense of balance and calm. And it’s a great counterpose to the commonly practiced Chaturanga Dandasana (Four-Limbed Staff Pose).

If you have serious wrist, shoulder, or neck problems, practice this pose only under the guidance of an experienced teacher. You’ll need a chair, a block, and a wall to practice some of these preparatory poses.

Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Rotate your thighs inward, big toes in, heels out, and press your palms to the floor slightly behind your buttocks with your fingers pointing forward toward your feet. If your shoulders protest, you can turn your fingers outward.

Bend your elbows and sink or hollow your front torso, spreading your scapulas as far away from your spine as possible. Rotate your upper arms inward and widen your elbows, letting the heads of your upper arm bones (humeri) jut forward. Enjoy the stretch between the scapulas for a minute or so.

Then straighten your elbows and lift your chest while leaving your lower body on the floor. Often, students simply squeeze their scapulas together and shove their lower front ribs forward, which hardens the front torso, restricting the free flow of breath, and compresses the low back. Instead, keep your scapulas wide and front torso soft.

Press the bases of your index fingers into the floor and hug your triceps against your humeri. As your elbows straighten out and your chest lifts, maintain the inward rotation of your upper arms, which will help the scapulas stay broad. Release your head back slightly, but don’t fully extend the neck. Trace the stretch along your front torso from your pubis to your sternum (breastbone).

Imagine directing your inhalations into the space behind your sternum (“imagine” because there’s no lung there, just your heart), increasing the lift of your chest. With each exhalation, reaffirm the opposing movements of the inner hands (down against the floor) and scapulas (up against your back). Hold for a minute or two. Repeat two or three times, until you feel confident you’ll be able to recreate the inward rotation of the thighs and arms and the actions of the hands and scapulas while maintaining the soft front torso when called on to do so in the more challenging circumstances of the full pose.

Next, sit on the front edge of a chair with your knees bent, heels directly below your knees. Wrap your hands around the back edge of the seat (for this first part of the exercise your upper arms will naturally rotate outward), thumbs pointing outward (Figure 1).

Inhale and slowly lift your buttocks away from the seat until your thighs, torso, and head form one long diagonal line, with your arms more or less perpendicular to the chair seat. Rotate your thighs slightly inward, and push (but don’t physically move) your knees away from your torso. The thigh rotation will tend to make your tailbone sag toward the floor, collapsing your belly, so firm your tailbone against your back pelvis and lengthen it. Hold this position for a minute, then sit back on the chair. On an inhalation, release the back edge of the seat and return to sitting upright. Take a few breaths.

If you like, repeat this exercise with your fingers turned forward, palms on the seat, and your upper arms rotated inward. Hold for one minute, release on an exhalation, and rest.

If you want to take this exercise to its limit, lift your buttocks again and extend your legs. Do your right leg first. Inhale and press out through your heel to straighten your knee, but suspend your foot a few inches off the floor. Then rotate your thigh inward, point your toes, and bring your sole to the floor. Just as the bases of your index forgers press the seat, so the base of your big toe presses on the floor. Repeat with the left leg. Once again, hold for a minute and release on an exhalation.

If you want to continue, brace the back legs of a chair against the wall and lay your block on the seat (if you’re using a wood block, cover the seat with a sticky mat to keep the block from sliding). Set the block on either its lowest or middle height near the front edge of the seat.

Sit on the floor right in front of the chair, knees bent, feet on the floor, heels 12 to 15 inches away from your buttocks, and lean back against the front edge of the seat. Press your hands on the floor with your fingers turned either forward, to the sides, or back—you choose—just in front of the feet of the chair legs.

Inhale and do what you did for the first part of the first exercise: Lift your thighs and torso parallel to the floor (heels below the knees), and then release your head back onto the block to take any pressure off your neck. If the block is too high or too low, come down and readjust. If you are having trouble opening your chest, it may help to reinforce the firmness of your palms against the floor, your scapulas against your back, and your triceps against the humeri. Then again, it may not.

Don’t get discouraged. Just practice this exercise every other day or so for the next few weeks, and you’ll be surprised how quickly things improve. Whatever happens, hold the pose for 30 seconds to a minute, then release to the floor on an exhalation. Smile.

If you can’t boost your chest, though, trying to extend your legs will probably make matters worse, so I don’t recommend it. But if your chest is reasonably lifted, then it’s acceptable to extend your legs.

Having trouble getting the balls of your feet, especially the bases of your big toes, on the floor? Position a rolled-up sticky mat on the floor where the balls of your feet will be when your legs are extended and press against that.

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. Cathay Pacific consistently ranks among the world's top airlines for business class. The A350-1000 is their flagship long-haul aircraft, featuring a 1-2-1 configuration with every single seat having direct aisle access. There are no middle seats. There are no awkward climbs over sleeping strangers. There is a full dine-on-demand menu, a curated wine list, noise-canceling headphones, and a ground service team that treats you like a valued guest before you even board. For the FI traveler, this redemption represents something rare: a genuine luxury experience — the kind that recalibrates your sense of what travel can feel like — made nearly free through a well-understood system. The math works. The experience delivers. And once you've done it, you'll understand exactly why the ChooseFI community talks about this one.

Alaska Mileage Plan is one of the most valuable frequent flyer programs in the world despite being a relatively small airline. The secret is their partner award chart: Alaska uses fixed pricing for partner airline awards, meaning costs do not fluctuate with demand the way dynamic programs do. This creates structural pricing inefficiencies — especially on premium cabin routes to Asia and Oceania — that savvy travelers can exploit. Alaska has partnerships with Cathay Pacific, Qantas, Japan Airlines, Emirates, Fiji Airways, and others. The primary way to earn Alaska miles is through the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card (Bank of America), through flying, or via Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio.

Here's the insight that transforms this from "interesting" to "actionable": Alaska Airlines Mileage Plan uses a fixed partner award chart, and that chart prices Cathay Pacific Business Class to Australia at 55,000 miles one-way — a number that hasn't kept pace with the explosive cash price inflation of premium cabin fares.

Most major U.S. loyalty programs have migrated to dynamic pricing, where award costs fluctuate with cash fare demand. Alaska hasn't done this for partner awards. Their chart is fixed. That means when Cathay Pacific's cash fares spike to $12,000 during Australian school holidays or peak summer travel, your award cost stays exactly where it was: 55,000 miles. This is the pricing inefficiency at the heart of this redemption, and it's why the ChooseFI community treats Alaska Mileage Plan as one of the most valuable programs in the industry.

Alaska Mileage Plan has only one meaningful transfer partner for most people: Marriott Bonvoy, at a ratio of 3 Bonvoy points to 1 Alaska mile. That's a steep ratio — you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points to generate 55,000 Alaska miles — and transfer times run 1 to 5 days, so plan accordingly. There is no direct credit card transfer path into Alaska Mileage Plan from Chase, Amex, or Citi, which is why the "Easy to Earn" score for this redemption is a 2 out of 5. The miles must be earned directly: through Alaska's co-branded credit card (the Alaska Airlines Visa from Bank of America), through flying Alaska or its partners, or via Marriott transfer.

This is crucial and often overlooked. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on any partner award bookings. This matters enormously for a Cathay Pacific redemption. If you were to book the same Cathay flight through Cathay's own Asia Miles program or through British Airways Avios, you could face fuel surcharges of $400–$900 or more on top of the points cost. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket cost is taxes and fees only — typically in the range of $50–$150 depending on the routing. That's it. A $12,000 experience for 55,000 miles and roughly $100 in fees.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit that is genuinely rare among U.S. programs. On the LAX–HKG–SYD routing, this means you can build a stopover in Hong Kong at no additional points cost. Spend a few days exploring one of the world's most dynamic cities — the markets of Mong Kok, the skyline from Victoria Peak, the dim sum temples of Kowloon — then board your continuing flight to Sydney. Two destinations. One redemption. Same 55,000 miles.

The 55,000-mile rate applies to both Cathay Pacific and Qantas for business class to Australia. Cathay routes you through Hong Kong (HKG); Qantas has its own metal and routing options. If Cathay availability is thin, checking Qantas can open up alternatives without changing your points cost.

Do not start at Alaska's website. Alaska's own search tool for partner availability can be unreliable for Cathay Pacific. Instead, go to ba.com (British Airways' booking site) and run a one-way business class search for your desired route — for example, LAX to SYD or LAX to HKG. British Airways and Cathay Pacific are oneworld partners, and BA's search engine surfaces Cathay award availability with remarkable accuracy. Look for "Reward" seats in the business class (Club World or equivalent) cabin. Any dates showing availability on BA.com are almost certainly bookable through Alaska as well. Screenshot or note the specific dates before moving on.

Alaska opens its award booking window 331 days in advance. If you're targeting peak travel dates — Australian summer (December–February), for example — set a calendar reminder to search and transfer 331 days ahead. Your miles also never expire in Mileage Plan, which gives you flexibility to accumulate without pressure.

Confirm you have at least 55,000 Alaska miles available. If you're converting Marriott Bonvoy points, you'll need 165,000 Bonvoy points at the 3:1 ratio. Initiate transfers at least one week before you plan to call, as Marriott-to-Alaska transfers can take 1 to 5 days.

Log into your Marriott Bonvoy account, navigate to "Transfer Points," select Alaska Airlines as the recipient program, and enter your Mileage Plan number. Transfer in increments of 3,000 Bonvoy points (yielding 1,000 Alaska miles). Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1 — points transfers are generally non-reversible.

This redemption cannot be booked online — Alaska's web portal does not support all partner award bookings, particularly for Cathay Pacific. Call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522. Tell the agent:

Have your Mileage Plan number, passport information, and a credit card for the taxes and fees ready. The call typically takes 20–40 minutes. Agents are generally knowledgeable, but if you encounter confusion, politely ask for a senior agent or call back.

If Cathay availability is limited on your preferred dates, ask the agent to check Qantas availability to Australia at the same 55,000-mile rate. Qantas Business (The Business) has its own award inventory and may have open seats when Cathay is fully allocated.

If you're routing through Hong Kong on Cathay, explicitly ask the agent to add a free stopover at HKG. This is a program benefit, not a favor — Alaska's routing rules allow one free stopover on one-way awards. Specify how many nights you want in Hong Kong before the continuing flight to Sydney.

The best way to find Cathay Pacific Business Class award availability is through the British Airways website (ba.com). Search for one-way flights from your U.S. gateway to Sydney or Melbourne, and look for dates showing Cathay Pacific-operated flights with Business Class availability. British Airways shows oneworld partner availability more reliably than most tools.

If Cathay Pacific shows no availability on your preferred dates, search for Qantas Business Class on the same route. Qantas availability can be found through the Qantas website or through British Airways. The Alaska Mileage Plan price is the same 55,000 miles for either carrier.

Earn miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa card sign-up bonus (typically 60,000 to 75,000 miles), through flying Alaska or partners, or by transferring from Marriott Bonvoy. If transferring from Marriott, allow 1 to 5 business days for the transfer to complete before your booking window closes.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522 and request a partner award booking on Cathay Pacific (or Qantas) Business Class. Provide your desired dates and routing. Ask about adding a free stopover in Hong Kong if routing through HKG. The agent will process the booking and deduct 55,000 miles plus taxes and fees (typically $50 to $150).

After booking through Alaska, manage your seat selection directly through the Cathay Pacific website or app using your booking reference. Select a window or aisle seat in the 1-2-1 configuration — every seat has direct aisle access, so there is no wrong choice. You can also pre-order meals and manage other preferences through Cathay's platform.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner want to celebrate a milestone — a sabbatical, a paid-off mortgage, financial independence itself — with a trip to Sydney. Here's exactly how this redemption plays out.

The Route: Los Angeles (LAX) → Hong Kong (HKG) → Sydney (SYD), on Cathay Pacific Business Class, with a 3-night stopover in Hong Kong.

Cash Price: A quick search on Google Flights confirms what you suspected — this itinerary in business class retails for approximately $8,000 per person during the shoulder season. During the Australian summer or holiday periods, it climbs closer to $11,000–$12,000.

Your Cost: 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles + approximately $85 in taxes and fees. Per person.

CPP Calculation: At $8,000 cash value, your 55,000 miles are worth 14.5 cents per point — more than seven times what you'd get redeeming Alaska miles for domestic economy. At $12,000, you're at 21.8 cents per point, which is among the highest CPP figures available anywhere in the U.S. loyalty ecosystem.

In Hong Kong, Cathay Pacific's The Pier Business Class Lounge awaits during your stopover travel. It's widely regarded as one of the finest airport lounges in the world — noodle bar, live cooking stations, a spa treatment center, and a wine selection that rivals dedicated restaurants.

After three days exploring Hong Kong, you reboard for the six-hour SYD leg, arriving in Sydney ready — genuinely ready, not depleted — to start your adventure.

Total cost for two: 110,000 Alaska miles + roughly $170 in fees. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: extraordinary experiences made nearly free through a system anyone can learn.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days out. Cathay Pacific releases business class award space to partner programs in limited quantities, and the best dates disappear quickly. Set a calendar alert for 331 days before your target travel date and be ready to search — and call — that morning.

The single best technique for this redemption: run your search on ba.com before calling Alaska. BA's search engine is faster, more reliable for Cathay availability, and lets you visually scan a full month of dates. Identify two or three date options before you pick up the phone. This dramatically shortens your call time and reduces the chance of getting an agent who says "I'm not seeing anything."

Don't treat the Hong Kong stopover as a layover — treat it as a destination. Alaska's routing rules explicitly allow a free stopover on one-way awards. Two to four nights in Hong Kong costs you nothing extra in miles. Pair this with a cheap positioning flight or use it as an anchor for a broader Asia itinerary.

This is the most common and most painful mistake. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers are generally not reversible. If you transfer 165,000 Bonvoy points to Alaska and then discover no award space exists on your dates, you're stuck with miles you may not use optimally. Always confirm availability on ba.com before initiating any transfer.

Book two one-way redemptions rather than a round-trip. This gives you full flexibility on return routing — you might come back on Qantas through another city, or extend your trip without penalty.

Since there are no major flexible currency transfer paths into Alaska (no Chase, Amex, or Citi transfers), the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature from Bank of America is your most efficient earning vehicle. The welcome bonus alone can cover a significant portion of this redemption. Pair with everyday spending in categories that earn elevated miles.

If Cathay availability is closed on your dates, Qantas Business Class to Australia prices at the same 55,000 miles. Qantas' "The Business" product on their A380 Sydney routes is exceptional in its own right — and availability patterns differ from Cathay, so checking both genuinely doubles your options.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI-minded couple or solo traveler who is willing to invest some effort in the booking process in exchange for an extraordinary, nearly free experience. If you've been dreaming about Australia and refuse to pay $8,000–$12,000 for a business class ticket — but you're also not willing to spend 20+ hours crammed in economy for a trip this significant — this is your answer.

Minimum requirements: You need 55,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per person. For two travelers, that's 110,000 miles. If you're building from zero through the Alaska Visa, factor in 6–12 months of earning runway before booking.

Within a broader FI travel strategy, this redemption pairs well with a Marriott Bonvoy credit card for point accumulation and an Alaska Visa for direct mile earning. It's a medium-complexity move with a very high ceiling on value.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is honest. It's not complicated in concept, but it has two specific friction points that trip up even experienced travel rewards enthusiasts. **Challenge 1: Earning the Miles** Alaska Mileage Plan's isolation from major flexible currency programs (no Chase Ultimate Rewards, no Amex Membership Rewards, no Citi ThankYou transfers directly) means you can't simply funnel points you already have into Alaska. The primary path is the Alaska Airlines Visa (Bank of America) or a Marriott Bonvoy conversion at an unfavorable 3:1 ratio. Plan your earning strategy well in advance. **Tip:** Prioritize the Alaska Visa signup bonus as your foundation, then supplement with Marriott points if needed. **Challenge 2: The Phone Booking Requirement** You cannot book this online. The call-in process intimidates people who've only ever booked travel digitally. **Tip:** Do your homework on ba.com first, have your dates ready, and approach the call as an informed customer — not someone asking for help finding availability. Agents respond well to specific, prepared callers. **Challenge 3: Cathay Award Availability** Cathay Pacific releases partner award space selectively and often in small quantities. Availability rated 3/5. **Tip:** Search exactly at the 331-day booking window, keep Qantas as your backup at the same price point, and be flexible with travel dates by even one or two days — a Tuesday departure often has inventory when Saturday doesn't. The good news: once you've done this once, you'll understand the system deeply enough to replicate it. The ChooseFI community has members who've booked this exact route multiple times. The first time takes effort. After that, it's a process you know cold.

The fastest path is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card from Bank of America, which typically offers a 60,000 to 75,000-mile sign-up bonus. That alone nearly covers the 55,000 miles needed. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at 3:1 (165,000 Bonvoy points equals 55,000 Alaska miles) or earn miles through flying Alaska and its partners.

Yes. You would book two separate one-way awards at 55,000 miles each. You could fly Cathay Pacific one direction and Qantas the other, or mix carriers based on availability. Each one-way can include its own free stopover.

Cathay Pacific typically releases Business Class award space 90 to 330 days before departure. The sweet spot for finding availability is usually 90 to 120 days out, when airlines release unsold premium cabin seats. Check frequently, as availability can appear and disappear quickly.

Alaska allows one free stopover on one-way awards. On a routing from the US to Australia via Hong Kong, you can stop in Hong Kong for any number of days at no additional miles cost. Simply tell the agent when booking that you want a stopover in HKG. This effectively gives you two destinations for the price of one redemption.

The Alaska Mileage Plan redemption for Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class to Australia is one of the most extraordinary sweet spots in travel rewards. At 55,000 miles for a seat that costs $5,000 to $12,000 in cash — with zero fuel surcharges and a free stopover in Hong Kong — this redemption delivers 9 to 22 cents per point. It requires more planning and effort than a simple hotel booking, but the payoff is a genuine luxury travel experience that proves the asymmetric value the FI community builds its travel rewards strategy around.

#8915. 5 Yin Yoga Poses for (Practically) Instant Calm

Katie McGrath is a certified yin yoga instructor. She leads classes on her YouTube channel, Yin Yoga with Katie, and offers invaluable advice on YJ as well. Here, she shares five yin yoga poses to help relieve stress so you can find calmness.

Some days bring more stress than others. Perhaps you have stopped (or have yet to start) working yet your jaw is tight, your breath sits high in your chest, and lying down does nothing except give your mind a quiet room in which to be loud.

Yin yoga is useful here for one very practical reason: yin yoga poses hold you close to the ground for several minutes. There is nothing to coordinate and nothing to balance. That combination gives your body and mind—and, more specifically, your nervous system—time to register that you’re in a safe place to release stress, which is something that, depending on you and your circumstances, a faster practice doesn’t always accomplish.

Stay in each of the following yin yoga poses for 3 to 5 minutes—and remember that a longer hold is not necessarily “better.” Aim for roughly 50 to 60 percent of the sensation you could create, which is a line in the sand rather than something carved in stone. If a pose feels exceptionally loud in your body, back off.

As you hold each pose encourage your exhale to become longer than your inhale. This is a simple and effective way to trigger your parasympathetic nervous system. In between the poses, lie flat for about a minute. You can stay still and do nothing or wiggle your body, it’s your choice. That minute is part of the practice, not just a gap in between the poses.

Practicing yoga for stress is not a cure. Instead, it is a way of placing your body in a position where settling down becomes a lot more likely. You might not feel dramatically different, and that is fine. Calm usually feels quieter than we expect it to be. What you are really after is a body that is slightly less braced than it was prior to your practice.

Gather what you have: a bolster or a firm cushion, two blankets, one or two yoga blocks, and a wall. If you have an eye pillow, feel free to use it.

What it does: This is a gentle, fully supported version of Child’s Pose that crosses into restorative yoga, a close cousin of yin yoga. The head makes contact with something solid, which many people find settling on its own. This shape also closes the body inward, which is useful when you want less input rather than more.

How to: Kneel with your knees wide and your big toes touching. Place a bolster lengthways between your thighs and lie your torso down over it. Turn your head to one side. Halfway through your hold, turn it the other way to stretch your neck evenly.

Add more props: Place a block under the far end of the bolster for more support and something solid to rest your head on. If your hips do not reach your heels, add a folded blanket between your calves and your backside, or place a yoga block under your hips. If your knees object to the shape of this pose, lie on your back and hug your knees toward your chest instead. For a more stretch-focused, yin yoga version of this pose, try it without the props.

Hold: Stay here for a total of 4 minutes, two with your head facing each direction.

What it does: This supine twist releases the lower back and the outer hips. And because you are on your back, it asks almost nothing of you but to surrender to gravity.

How to: Lie on your back. Draw both knees toward your chest, then let them fall toward the right. Take your arms out wide. Let your head turn toward the left, if that is comfortable, or keep it neutral as you face the ceiling.

Add props: Place a bolster or folded blanket underneath the knees, if needed, so that they land on something supportive rather than hanging in space. If your right shoulder lifts off the floor, prop it with a folded blanket instead of constantly forcing it toward the mat. If your lower back complains, lower the knees less close to the ground.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: This supported backbend opens your chest and ribcage, which both spend most of the day closed. When the chest is open in Fish Pose, your breath can expand more freely.

How to: Place a yoga block on its lowest level behind you on the mat. For more support, have a second block ready to rest your head on. Lie back onto the block, aligning the bottom of your shoulder blades with one edge. Rest the back of your head on the second block or bring the crown of your head to the mat. Let your arms fall open at your sides. Keep your legs long or you can bend your knees and keep your feet on the mat.

Add props: Add a bolster underneath your knees or, for more of a hip stretch, touch the soles of the feet together and let your knees fall to the sides, tucking cushions underneath your outer thighs. If your lower back is uncomfortable, try lying back over a bolster placed lengthways instead. If your head tips back quite a lot and your throat feels exposed, add a small cushion underneath your head.

Hold: Stay here for 4 minutes. Come out slowly, and rest before you move on.

What it does: This shape offers lateral flexion, also known as a side stretch, which is the direction almost nobody moves during ordinary life. Banana Pose lengthens the body along your outer torso, including the muscles between the ribs, so that your ribcage has more room to expand when you breathe in.

How to: Lie on your back with your legs long. Before you move anything, notice that the backs of both hips are on the floor and level, and try to keep your hips in the center of the mat. Walk both feet to the right, as far as they’ll go without the right hip lifting. Reach your arms overhead and walk both hands toward the right, taking hold of your left wrist with your right hand if that is comfortable and available to you. If you want a more intense side stretch, cross your right ankle over your left. Soften your jaw and let the breath move into the long side of your body.

Add props: No props needed here! Skip the ankle cross if the outer hip is the loudest thing in the pose. If your arms do not want to go overhead, rest them wherever they are comfortable.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: Legs Up the Wall finds the legs are supported and the spine is flat, so it is a good place to stop. It’s also one of the most effective restorative poses for activating your parasympathetic nervous system, allowing for real and accessible relaxation.

How to: Sit sideways with one hip against the wall, then swing your legs up as you lie back. Shuffle your backside close to the wall, or a few inches away if that suits your hamstrings better. Rest your hands on your belly or out to the sides.

Add props: For extra comfort, slide a folded blanket under your hips if your lower back feels flat and strained. If your feet tingle, bend your knees or come down for a moment.

Hold: Stay here for 5-10 minutes or for as long as you need.

Extract yourself from each shape slowly and with care. To finish your practice, find your way to a comfortable seat and breathe here with your eyes closed (or your gaze soft) for 1-3 minutes. Give yourself a moment before you reach for your phone.

#8912. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8911. Inside an Elite Running Group’s Marathon Training Strategies That Get Them to the Front of the Pack

Go inside the Boulder-based team helping Hellen Obiri, Joe Klecker, and others chase NYC success, and learn how their approach can improve your own training.

Six years ago, when Joe Klecker was named to the inaugural class of the On Athletics Club (OAC) in Boulder, Colorado, his goals were all about racing fast on the track. But based on his physiology, his tenacity, and even his genes, coach Dathan Ritzenhein already knew Klecker was destined to become a marathoner—and probably a very good one.

When the team now known as OAC Global formed in the summer of 2020, it featured eight postcollegiate runners chasing Olympic berths from 1,500 to 10,000 meters. The OAC sent several runners (including Klecker) to the Tokyo Olympics and brought home medals from Paris.

But track success was only the first step of what Ritzenhein envisioned. In the years since, he and coach Laura Thweatt have built an elite marathon program, too.

Kenyan great Hellen Obiri, four-time Major Marathon winner and current women’s New York City Marathon course record holder, put OAC on the marathon map after joining in 2022. The progression of Klecker (with a marathon PR of 2:05:56 from Boston), along with newer teammates Ryan Ford (2:05:46 marathon PR) and Patrick Kiprop (59:14 half marathon PR), has helped to solidify the team’s presence on the roads.

As all four prepare for the NYC Marathon, we went behind the curtain at the OAC Global Training Facility in Boulder to learn what has fueled their success.

When On recruited Obiri to Boulder in 2022, the two-time Olympic silver medalist at 5,000 meters was about to move up to the marathon. That meant shifting from pure track speed and relatively low mileage (80 miles per week) to 120- to 125-mile weeks and grinding sessions like 25K tempo runs.

With no other marathoners on the team, she did portions of her long runs with 10,000-meter runner Alicia Monson and some longer tempo efforts and fartleks with Klecker. All three benefited.

Obiri became one of the best marathoners in the world, winning New York and Boston twice and an Olympic bronze medal in Paris; Monson broke the American 5,000- and 10,000-meter records in 2023, and Klecker got a taste of what marathon training was all about, which gave him proper perspective as he was about to begin his first marathon build.

“[Obiri’s] level is so high that, on a lot of our long runs and even some fartleks, we would overlap for a good chunk of those workouts,” Klecker, 29, tells Runner’s World. “And for me, it was harder than I thought. When you’re racing on the track, a long run is kind of a chill day because all of your hard work is on the track. But when you’d see her go out and do her long runs, she was just hammering from the start, and so I knew I really had to wrap my head around this new way of training for the roads.”

As Klecker got closer to his marathon debut last fall, the OAC signed Ford as his primary training partner. They developed a synergy, but weren’t entirely aligned in their schedules because Ford was building up to the Chicago Marathon and Klecker was preparing for New York a month later. But they did sync up for all of their training (including harder workouts) as they prepared for Boston, and that paid off with better racing execution and significant time drops.

The team recently added an even faster teammate in Kiprop, a 25-year-old Kenyan and former University of Arkansas star, after big wins at the Lilac Bloomsday 12K and Peachtree Road Race 10K. He ran 59:14 in his half marathon debut in January in Houston and moved to Boulder in early August to join Klecker and Ford at the start of the 12-week New York buildup.

Klecker admits his marathon debut was mostly about surviving 26 miles. He trained to run a measured race holding 5:00 pace the whole way. That meant he fell off the lead pack when surging began along First Avenue, but his strength allowed him to reel in runners who were fading in the final miles.

This year, the trio of Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop have been able to push each other on hard long runs and marathon-specific workouts aimed at mimicking the surges and inconsistent pacing at the front of the pack in New York City.

“This year, the goal is to be up front and try to race for that podium and not just catch the people who die. You can’t do that from two minutes back late in the race,” Klecker says. “Now, based on the training we’ve done through a natural progression of workouts, it feels I should be ready to go with some moves. That's kind of been the whole focus of the past year, to be more competitive throughout the race.”

Training with the team has worked well for Obiri, 36, who is coming off a personal best 2:15:53 runner-up effort at the London Marathon in April. But at times, she has had a penchant to run too hard in training with faster teammates, which is why OAC has recruited seasonal training partners closer to her pace from Kenya over the past two years. (This year, it is Dennis Kipkosgeu, a 2:13 marathoner.)

She heads to New York as the defending champion after what she considers her best buildup yet.

“The growth of our road running team feels amazing because I have runners to train with every day,” she says of the OAC team. “When I joined in 2022, I was the only marathoner, and that was hard. This gives me confidence because there are four of us working so hard together.”

By early 2025, Ritzenhein wanted a coach to lead the road program day to day while he and assistant coach Kelsey Quinn stayed focused on the track group that included Yared Nuguse, bronze medalist in the 1500 at the Paris Olympics.

Thweatt, a longtime Boulder runner, had just retired from her own pro career and posted on Instagram that she was looking for new opportunities. Two days later, Ritzenhein called her. Within about two weeks, she was the OAC’s marathon coach.

A 2:25:38 marathoner who twice finished fifth at the U.S. Olympic Trials (in the marathon in 2020 and 10,000 meters in 2016) and notched top-10 finishes in London and New York, Thweatt admits she initially wasn’t sure what she could offer runners much faster than her. But early in the New York build, she ran with Obiri several days a week; as the workouts got faster, she paced her from a bike.

Thweatt quickly learned the role of a coach is more than just explaining and monitoring workouts and more about sharing experiences, reducing stressors, instilling confidence, visualizing race-day situations, keeping athletes focused on the process, and making sure they run easy enough on their easy days—all key elements of marathon training.

The runners are doing the work in training, but a coach is the glue that brings it all together, Thweatt says, and that’s true for any level of runner.

Kiprop says he has relied on the experience of his coaches and teammates during this first marathon build, so much so that he believes his entry into racing 26.2 miles might be easier than most. He heads to New York with a new level of fitness and plenty of firsthand course knowledge and pre-race logistics from Klecker, Obiri, Ford, Thweatt, and Ritzenhein, who all ran their first marathons on the five-borough course.

“At first, I didn’t know if I could handle the training for the marathon,” he says. “But with time, as you train together, you build that confidence, you build the courage to face the marathon.”

Ritzenhein signed on as the OAC’s first coach just weeks after his last pro race in early 2020, eager to build a program that would span more than a single Olympic cycle. He knew that would require patience, a supportive team atmosphere, and top-tier facilities.

Today, the OAC Global roster has 20 athletes from eight countries and operates out of its own 10,000-square-foot training center eight miles north of downtown Boulder, opened in 2024. It’s the nerve center for everything the team does: training, fueling, strength work, and communications. But it also serves as a place to develop camaraderie and team chemistry, which can help athletes thrive in a marathon training block, instead of just surviving.

“I think coming up with this facility was a genius idea,” Kiprop says. “It has everything we need. It’s nice to have your team around you here. When we’re together, it feels like family.”

The facility has two antigravity treadmills, eight Woodway treadmills, an underwater treadmill, and e-stim machines—most of which they use when there’s inclement weather and for rehab. There are treatment tables for massage therapists and physiotherapists, meeting space for sessions with coaches, dietitians, and mental strength counselors, and a lounge with a mini kitchen stocked with drinks, snacks, and supplements.

They also have a full gym with space for strength training, drills, and strides, an important part of their training, as marathon preparation is more than just running for the OAC crew. The team’s strength coaches, Jason Ross and Joslynn Peterson, have the runners do a wide range of running-specific and general strength exercises twice a week.

Most of the strength workouts focus on tissue health with longer isometrics (holding an exercise in one position as you would in a plank) at the beginning of a training cycle and then progress to increased weight and fewer reps, Ross tells Runner’s World. While each athlete has individual exercises to tackle, some of the common strength moves include weighted box step-ups, single-leg bent-knee hamstring isometric holds, trap bar deadlifts, landmine single-leg Romanian deadlifts, seated calf raises, and weighted standing calf raise isometrics.

“You cannot be complacent on that side of things,” Thweatt says. “It makes a huge difference. It’s an equal part of training. You need to make sure that everyone’s staying healthy and strong.”

Working alongside sports dietitians, each OAC marathoner has dialed in an individual fueling plan based on sweat testing and data from training. They know how many calories they burn on their long runs and hardest sessions, how much fluid and sodium they lose in their sweat, and exactly what they need to replace during a long run or hard session so they finish strong instead of fading late.

The exact details of what each runner needs are slightly different, Thweatt says, but they’re adept at consuming gels on the run and have practiced grabbing bottles off of tables, so they know how long they need to carry them and drink from them for optimal fueling.

“Fueling is one of the biggest things we drive home during training,” Thweatt says. “We’ve gone through the fueling plan in almost every training session that we do and we practice it like it’s going to be on race day. They know what’s going into their bottles on race day, so hopefully when we get to race day, it’s not even something they really have to think about because it’s what they’ve been doing for the last 12 weeks.”

While most runners prepare for marathons on a seven-day cycle, the OAC marathon group mostly used a nine-day schedule during this year’s 12-week buildup to both Boston and New York. No two weeks start or finish the same, but it’s a cycle with room for three long or hard sessions with two or three days of easier running in between—especially important while training at 5,400 feet, Thweatt says.

“The nine-day schedule just made sense because at altitude, with as hard as they’re running our harder sessions, we just need to make sure that we’re absorbing that training—not losing the recovery piece of it,” she explains.

At the peak of the New York build, the OAC runners logged 118 to 135 miles per week, depending on each runner’s preference and background. Klecker started his training early in July to boost his volume and eventually pushed his max to more than 130 miles a few times this fall. Ford and Obiri found their sweet spot around 120, and Kiprop, who previously averaged 100, settled in at about 110.

The biggest pieces of that volume were 35K (22-mile) and 40K (25-mile) long runs, including a couple of them at 8,500 feet on Magnolia Road west of Boulder. On the four 40K runs late in the block, Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop started at about 5:45 mile pace and worked down to 5:30 through 20K, then progressed to 5:20 for most of the final 20K, often closing near 5:00 pace.

Thweatt calls those long runs the bread and butter of the OAC training, but the key is balancing that volume and the harder, faster workouts with slower running on easy days.

After those key long runs, the OAC athletes typically run about six miles “super easy,” Thweatt says, which for them usually means as slow as 7:15 pace but as fast as 6:45 pace. Thweatt has been trying to make sure the athletes (especially Klecker and Obiri) run at those paces on their easy days to ensure they’re optimizing recovery.

The next day, the runners log double sessions of 10 miles in the morning and five miles in the afternoon, followed the next day by 12 miles in the morning and six miles in the afternoon. Those low-key maintenance runs give the mind and body a break, setting them up for one of their signature spicier workouts.

“So between big long runs or bigger sessions, we usually give them three easy days,” Thweatt says. “So you’re not touching those faster paces for three days, but you’re still getting that good quality time on feet and making sure the body is absorbing that last hard session before we hit it again with another one. Recovery is so important and it’s a piece not everyone likes to talk about as much because it's not as flashy as the big workout days.”

Two other staples of the team’s NYC build-up included 10- to 12-mile tempo runs and long, hard fartleks. The tempo runs usually start at 5:00 pace and get faster (Kiprop recently closed one at 4:45 pace), while a sample fartlek alternates “1K on” (2:50-2:55, or 4:35-4:40 mile pace) and “1K off” (3:10, or 5:05 mile pace).

“It’s about being uncomfortable for long periods of time and still trying to shift gears at the end to remind them what it’s going to be like in the marathon,” Thweatt says. “We’re trying to mirror the surges of a marathon in our workouts.”

In the final weeks, the runners also did several VO2 max sessions on the track, including two sets of 1600, 1200, 800, and 400 meters at about 5K pace, which for the OAC’s men comes out to 4:20, 3:12, 2:06, and 1:02, with the second set slightly quicker.

That kind of work has been a big change for Ford, but it has paid off.

“I was somebody that would try to approach marathon training by running at marathon pace and get really comfortable with that. But I think that only works to a certain extent,” says Ford, who just turned 29. “When I was running 2:08 to 2:09, I’d kind of be off of the pack running my own race. Now I am able to stay with the front pack and compete better.”

Unlike Chicago, Berlin, London, or Valencia, which involve mostly flat courses you can run at an even pace, the New York City Marathon is on a rolling course and pace surges play a big role in how the race plays out, Thweatt says.

Ritzenhein and Thweatt believe runners aiming for success in New York have to be able to tap into quicker-cadence running on a moment’s notice to match the terrain and competitive pickups. For example, while runners will do much of the first 16 miles at an even pace, it’s not uncommon for the lead packs to get split apart by frontrunners ratcheting up the pace (often sub-4:25 for men and sub-5:15 for women) on the 3.5-mile rolling, slightly uphill section along First Avenue on the way to the Bronx.

“Those fast track sessions in the middle to the end of a build allow us to spike the system so you can have that speed in the well for the moments you need to shift gears in a race,” Thweatt says. “With the marathon, especially with where the event is at right now with the depth and fast times, you have to touch that speed in training if you want to be competitive in the race. You can increase your volume and do longer workout sessions, but you can’t just do everything at threshold or marathon pace. It’s really important to keep that system firing and to keep it sharp so you have that speed when you need it.”

Ford credits the faster workouts for lowering his half marathon PR by 71 seconds in January (59:48) and his marathon PR by more than two minutes in Boston. He recently ran a 25K version of the 1K on/1K off fartlek, clocking a 1:03 half marathon in the middle of it.

“The reality is you’ll spend time running slower than marathon pace and you’ll spend time running faster [in New York],” he says. “Now that I’ve kind of reached this new level with the faster training with these guys, the approach is more like, ‘Let’s go to New York and try to compete with that front group.’”

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.
