#8869. Cycling Metrics Guide: What to Measure for Better Rides

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Confused about all the data? Learn what numbers to track to see your progress and improve your performance.

My favorite metric has always been feel. I trained for two Ironman, including World Championships in Kona and entire mountain bike stage races like Cape Epic and Brasil Ride tracking nothing but time, distance, speed, and how I felt. I’d trained enough with heart rate and power to know how they worked, but I always reverted to feel.

That said, there have certainly been races where I’ve blown up—where the implosion probably could have been prevented had I been watching my watts. And the times I did spend training with power, there’s little question my sessions were more precise and likely more productive. It can be easier to stay on track with training when you have measurable goals and quantifiable sessions.

Today, I strike a compromise between luddite and tech-geek, tracking my resting heart rate and heart rate variability with an Oura ring, and recording heart rate for most rides so I can keep an eye on how fatigued and/or fresh I am.

Ultimately, I think that’s the best process when it comes to using data. Start with the basics, then add on as you get more experience. Most riders end up settling on a handful of metrics they rely on most.

Here, a primer to get you started tracking your cycling metrics.

Obviously, tracking cycling metrics generally means you need a device to capture that data. Most of the metrics, such as speed, distance, time, and elevation, mentioned here can be captured with a GPS-enabled bike computer like a Garmin, Wahoo, Lezyne, or Hammerhead. The deeper you want to dive into the data, the more sensors you need.

Great for: The satisfaction of seeing your pace pick up

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

Your miles per hour (or kilometers per hour, depending on where you live) is a fun metric to track, and it can tell you broadly high much fitter you’re getting. The catch: It’s not very reliable to use in training because so many factors influence it. For example, you may be cranking out World Pro-level wattage but if you’re doing so into a 30-mph block headwind, you’re not going to be setting any land speed records.

Your average speed is best used as an indicator of how your training is going overtime: If you are now consistently averaging 16+ mph on a loop that you used to average 15+ mph, you can see you’re getting fitter and faster.

You can track your average time with and without your stopping time factored into the pace. Most people don’t factor stoppage (or “café time”) in because they want to see moving time only. But if you’re training for a big event like a gravel race, it’s important to know your average speed including that stoppage time, because races often set cut offs based on a 10-mph pace, which includes rest stops. Once you see how long those “short breaks” really are, you can learn to keep them quick and avoid missing time cuts. You’ll also know how fast you need to ride to allow yourself the stoppage time you plan to take.

Great for: Watching your endurance increase

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

We all like to see how far we’ve gone, especially on a big ride. Distance can be a motivational metric to track. If you’re averaging 50 to 80 miles a week, can you make it 100? Can you set an annual goal of hitting 5,000 miles or more? When tracking distance, it’s important to take into consideration what type of riding you do. Riding 60 miles on flat roads is very different from 60 miles of singletrack. One might take three to four hours while the other takes the better part of a day.

Distance is also important to track if you’re training for a ride of a specific distance. If you want to ride a century in the fall, you’ll want to work up to it by hitting 50-mile and 75-mile rides as the event approaches.

Great for: Learning pacing for eventsEquipment needed: Any watch will do, but a bike computer can automatically track moving time and stoppage time

Most cyclists train by time because that’s our most finite resource. How much time you have each week to ride determines how to best use that time if your goal is to improve performance. Riders with a tight time budget are best served doing polarized training that emphasizes short, hard interval workouts during the week and longer rides as time permits on the weekend.

Great for: Bragging rights and building strength (hills make you stronger!)

Equipment needed: A GPS enabled bike computer

Elevation gain in cycling is the total amount of feet (or meters) you climb over the course of a ride. Climbing is good training, because your body must work harder in the effort to overcome the pull of gravity. If you’re the kind of rider who routinely avoids inclines, setting climbing goals and tracking elevation can give your cycling fitness a boost. If your goal is to focus on elevations, start by aiming to hit an average of 500 feet per 10 miles. Work up to what some climbing lovers call the “golden ratio” of 1,000 feet of vertical gain per 10 miles of riding.

Equipment needed: Apps like Strava will estimate your calorie burn, but for more accurate data, use a heart rate monitor and/or power meter

A calorie is a unit of energy provided by food. The calorie metric provided on your cycling computer or smartwatch is how many of those units you used to complete your ride. But calorie calculations are an imperfect science.

Some devices will provide estimates based on algorithms, which are just that—estimates. Past research has shown that devices can have a wide margin of error: A Stanford study published in 2017 reported that not one of the seven devices they tested—including the Apple Watch, Fitbit Surge, Mio Alpha 2, Basis Peak, Microsoft Band, PulseOn, and the Samsung Gear S2—delivered an accurate number for calories burned. The most accurate one, the Apple Watch, was off by 27 percent. The least accurate one? Off by 93 percent.

A more recent meta-analysis published in The British Journal of Sports Medicine echoed these findings, indicating that though devices that measure your heart rate along with your movement are more accurate, they all have a pretty significant margin of error.

Apps like GarminConnect, Strava, and other training apps might be a bit better, but they’re not perfect, either, and the number they give you depends heavily on the information you give the app. The more detailed data you input about yourself, such as age, height, weight, gender, and max heart rate, the more accurately their internal algorithms can calculate your calorie burn. Wearing a chest-based heart rate monitor that is synced to your device also helps make your calorie count more accurate.

Ultimately, the best way to know how many calories you burn on a ride is by using a power meter. Power meters measure the work you’re performing and display it in kilojoules, which is a unit of work that takes into account that the human body isn’t 100-percent efficient when turning energy from your fuel stores into physical work, like pedaling a bike.

“Kilojoules and calories burned in cycling convert to a 1:1 ratio,” explains USA Cycling elite coach Daniel Matheny, head coach at Matheny Endurance in Colorado Springs. If your ride file says you performed 800 kJ of work, you can feel confident within a 5-percent margin of error that you burned about 800 calories.

Tracking calories is useful for helping you fuel for rides. Some riders underestimate the number of calories they’ll burn on a three-hour group ride and end up falling off the back on the verge of bonking three quarters of the way through. Properly fueled riders ride faster and happier.

Just note that the goal is not to replace every calorie you’re burning as you ride. Your gut can’t take that. “Replace about half the calories you’re burning per hour for rides lasting longer than three or four hours to keep fuel levels topped off,” says sports physiologist and SkratchLabs founder Allen Lim, Ph.D.

You may also notice that the fitter you become, the fewer calories you burn on a given ride at a given pace. That’s because your body has become more efficient at using oxygen.

Great for: Training leg strength and speed; watching fitness improve for new riders

Equipment needed: A cycling computer and cadence sensor

Cadence is the number of revolutions you spin per minute as you pedal. If you have a cadence sensor you can watch your cadence in real time on your bike computer and track your average cadence for each ride.

It’s debatable how useful it is to track and/or train cadence. Coaches used to recommend athletes aim to pedal 90 rpm, but research doesn’t really show benefits from forcing yourself to do so. In 2019, a team of British researchers found that not only did amateur riders not get any added benefit from high cadence cycling, but they also became less efficient, so they were wasting energy.

Hunter Allen, CEO of Peaks Coaching Group, and author of Training and Racing with a Power Meter explains that your cadence will be determined by two things: your main muscle fiber type and your level of cardiovascular cycling fitness. The balance of those factors (which, of course, can change over time) determine your ideal cadence.

Newer riders tend to pedal more slowly because their cardiovascular system can’t handle the higher heart rate that comes with high cadences. As fitness improves, cadence generally rises.

While you probably don’t need to track your cadence from ride to ride, if you have a cadence sensor, it can help you do cadence drills, such as low gear/high cadence and high gear/low cadence drills that can help build cardiovascular fitness, leg speed, and leg strength.

Great for: Learning what sustainable (and unsustainable) efforts feel like and tracking fitness improvement

Equipment needed: Your heart, lungs, legs, and brain

It doesn’t get any more basic than RPE, your rate of perceived exertion. Put more simply, it's a measure of how hard you feel like you’re working. On a 1 to 10 scale, 1 is coasting along on a flat road with a tailwind, and 10 is full gas, willing yourself not to vomit.

You can also think of this as your “breath analyzer,” because a monitoring your breathing is an easy way to rate your efforts. Your muscles use more oxygen the harder you push, so breathing rate is a direct indication of work. If you’re able to sing and recite poetry, you’re not working very hard. If you’re gasping uncontrollably, you are maxed out.

Research shows RPE works just as well as any scientific equipment for measuring your actual effort at any given time, but it doesn’t tell you much more. For instance, you may be huffing and puffing and battling burning legs, but barely producing any power; or you could be feeling chainless while cranking out major wattage. Though you can train by “feel” alone, you get a more complete picture of your daily sessions and progress if you pair it with other metrics like heart rate or power.

It also takes discipline to train by feel because you have to remain tuned in, and it’s all too easy to slack off when you should be pushing or push too hard on a recovery day.

Great for: Creating specific training zones and tuning into your freshness and/or fatigue

Equipment needed: A heart rate monitor and compatible bike computer or watch

As your effort increases, your heart pumps more oxygen and nutrient-rich blood to fuel your muscles. The result: Your heart rate goes up. Monitoring your heart beats per minute (BPM) with a heart rate monitor will tell you just how hard you’re working.

To use heart rate, you need to first determine your max heart rate (MHR)—or the highest number of BPM you can hit. Forget the generic 220 minus your age formula for determining max heart rate and take a field test instead:

Warm up thoroughly, then do a 10-minute time trial as hard as possible, kicking it into full throttle for the final 60 seconds, aiming to full on sprint the final 20 seconds. Cool down and check your data for MHR. Repeat two more times (with rest days in between) to find your true max. Once you have your max, you can break down various levels of training efforts according to percentages of that number. As you get fitter, you’ll be able to ride faster at lower heart rates.

Overall, heart rate monitoring is an excellent training tool—but there are a few downsides. For one, it’s a little fickle. Your BPM can drift up or down depending on how much coffee you’ve had (caffeine raises it); ambient temperature; your hydration status; your plasma volume; how rested you are; and where you are in your menstrual cycle. It can also drift up within the same ride, especially when it’s hot.

Pairing HR and RPE tracking gives you a more complete picture of your effort. If you’re performing tempo intervals at a target heart rate of 150 BPM and your RPE is around 5, you’re on the money. If you’re performing those same intervals but working at an RPE of 8 to hit that same heart rate, that’s a sign that you’re not recovered and should do an easier workout. There’s also some lag time between the moment you increase intensity and the moment your heart rate reflects it, so it’s not the best tool for high-intensity efforts.

You can monitor your heart rate with a chest strap or wrist-based heart rate monitor via your sports watch. Wrist-based sensors on smartwatches and fitness trackers can be less accurate for cyclists, according to some research. That may be due to the optical sensors having less consistent contact with our wrists as we bend it to grasp our bars.

Great for: The most accurate measure of your effort

Equipment needed: A power meter and a compatible bike computer

Power equals work over time. In cycling, your work rate is described as watts of energy produced: Being able to produce a lot of power for your size makes you faster on the bike. Monitoring your watts with a power meter gives you instant feedback about how hard you’re working.

Power training generally revolves around your functional threshold power, or the wattage you can produce for a one-hour time trial, which is a fundamental benchmark for fitness. A common protocol for determining your FTP is performing a 20-minute time trial and multiplying that average wattage by 0.95, since your hour-long wattage would be about 5 percent lower, according to Allen.

The beauty of power is that it is absolute: You are either producing 350 watts on those hill repeats, or you’re not. If you’re not hitting your intended watts for a given workout, it’s time to rest.

Though power is more precise than heart rate, it’s worthwhile to combine the two, as heart rate represents your body’s response to the work you’re doing. Your heart rate should rise and fall in line with your power output. When your power is low and your heart rate is high, it’s recovery time. If you’re serious about training to the point that you’ve hired a coach, a power meter is a good investment.

Great for: Understanding when you need more recovery time

Equipment needed: An Oura ring, Whoop strap, or specific HRV tracking device

HRV is a relatively new player in the performance tracking sphere. Unlike heart rate, which you watch in real time, HRV is one that you track once a day, preferably first thing in the morning (or if you wear an Oura ring or Whoop strap, you’ll see your average overnight score).

HRV is a good indicator of your recovery and/or readiness. It may seem counterintuitive, but a fit, rested, healthy heart should not beat consistently like a metronome. Instead, it should nimbly respond to input from your sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) nervous system.

High variability (reflected in a higher HRV score) shows that you’re ready to go and capable of adapting to your environment and respond to exercise demands to perform well. Low variability between beats can be a sign of stress, fatigue, and inflammation—all things that can follow training too hard with too little recovery.

HRV is specific to each person and naturally declines with age. Though high numbers are considered “better,” high is relative to your own baseline. One person’s high HRV might be 125 while another’s high might be 55.

Referenced regularly, HRV scores will help you track fitness gains. For example, you’ll typically see HRV measurements decrease (become more negative) during long, heavy training blocks. Then you should see a rebound, where your HRV is significantly higher, after a recovery period. An upward trend over time means you’re getting fitter. A downward trend means you’re training too hard and or under too much stress without proper rest and recovery. When using HRV, it’s important not to put too much weight on a single day’s reading, but rather to look at trends and averages over a few days.

You can buy individual HRV monitors like straps and finger clip sensors, but if you’re going to track HRV, you should also track resting heart rate, sleep, and training load and/or activity levels, so you can put it into context. So, a device like a Whoop strap or Oura ring are the way to go, because they automatically put HRV into context of the whole picture. (If you work with a coach, they can as well).

Do you need to track HRV to become a better rider? Of course not. You can generally tell when you need a rest day by feel. But if you routinely train hard and like to dial in your training and lifestyle habits for optimum recovery and training readiness, this is a useful metric to use. It can be especially helpful if you’re trying to establish healthy habits like cutting back on alcohol and getting more sleep, because those types of lifestyle factors show up quickly in HRV scores.

All this measuring and monitoring doesn’t do much good unless you apply it to specific training purposes—that is, training at different effort levels to build specific types of fitness. That’s where training zones come in. Different coaches break down training zones differently, but in general you’ll see effort levels spread out over five to seven zones that range from recovery to max effort. For example, here are five classic training zones:

You need to ride easy so your body can heal, adapt, and get stronger and fitter. Zone 1 rides should feel ridiculously easy. Your only goal is to boost your circulation and promote repair and recovery. These rides hover at one or two on the RPE scale.

Zone 2 is all about aerobic effort. Endurance rides require enough energy to feel like exercise, but still let you carry a conversation, cruise for hours, and enjoy the ride. These efforts stimulate mitochondrial growth and build capillaries and fat-burning capacity. Zone 2 rides are done at an RPE of three to four.

Efforts in Zone 3 are just above your comfort level, so you’re breathing faster and working harder than you would on a typical aerobic, endurance ride. You’re not working so hard, however, that you can’t sustain your effort for a long period of time. Steady Zone 3 tempo efforts improve your body’s ability to clear and use lactic acid, so they also help raise your lactate threshold. They’re done at an RPE of five to six.

If VO2 max is your roof, lactate threshold—the point at which you start working anaerobically—is your drop ceiling. Training in Zone 4, which is right at that point, helps you hit higher intensities before you bump into that overhang. These efforts are done at an RPE of seven to eight.

To raise your VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use, you need to push yourself as far into the red as you can go. Zone 5 efforts are done full throttle—a nine to 10 on the RPE scale. Because they’re so hard, they’re also very short, generally lasting three to five minutes.

Here is a sample of basic training zones that incorporate the metrics above. Some coaches will break these down and expand them further or use other metrics such as percent of lactate threshold heart rate as a guide.

How to Fit Cadence Training Into Your Schedule

#8866. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8863. The Best Cargo E-Bikes of 2026, Tested by Editors Who Used Them for Groceries, Kid Hauling, and Daily Commutes

From budget longtails to family-ready front-loaders, these picks can help replace car trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Each year, I ride many different bicycles. From high-performance road bikes to full suspension mountain bikes to basic hybrids, I’ve swung a leg over eight or ten styles of bicycles in the past six months. But switching to an electric cargo bike has made the biggest positive impact on my overall quality of life. Thanks to a cargo bike, I’ve been mostly car-free for the last several months.

Traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around. However, if you need to carry more than you can squeeze into a backpack or maybe some panniers, most commuter bikes or e-bikes aren’t up for the job. Common tasks like grocery shopping, carrying large items, or transporting children can be tough on even the best of them. That’s what makes cargo bikes great—they can carry everything (and more!) that you can imagine.

As their name suggests, cargo bikes are designed to carry heavy, large, or awkward loads. Their extra hauling capacity makes cargo bikes incredibly useful for families, commuters, and riders in cities, suburbs, and small towns across the country. Bicycle brands produce cargo bikes in several distinct layouts to meet the needs of riders seeking to carry or move more stuff by pedal power.

Almost any bicycle purpose-built to carry passengers or extra gear—such as packages, bags, or boxes—can be called a “cargo bike.” Cargo bikes typically feature reinforced frames, racks or mounting points, and come with higher payload capacities than traditional commuter, city, or townie bikes. Bike brands and third-party manufacturers also offer a wide array of accessories to outfit a cargo bike for your specific needs and use cases.

Bicycling’s editors are huge fans of cargo bikes, and we use them regularly for our daily commutes, running errands, dropping kids at school, and family rides. Like other bicycle types, cargo bikes come in all shapes and sizes—and there’s almost certainly one that’s perfect for you. Finally, while non-assisted cargo bikes are available, electric-assist cargo bikes are now far more common. So all of the models we test use electric motors.

Buying Tip: Consider where you will store your cargo bike. Their large size and extra weight can make cargo bikes difficult to store if you don’t have a garage or dedicated bike storage. If you need to park your cargo bike outside, get a heavy-duty bike lock and a bicycle cover to keep it safe.

Some cargo bikes are loaded with features but cost too much, while others are low-priced but don’t ride well. However, the Aventon Abound LR is the rare $2,000 electric cargo bike that doesn’t feel like a compromise—And that’s why it’s our Best Overall pick.

The Abound LR is built to handle daily life—daycare drop-offs and pickups, grocery runs, and commuting—without the premium price tag of its competitors. Plus, it rides with more polish than some bikes costing twice as much. This makes it a great option for families and utility‑minded riders. The LR can handle kids, panniers, and weekly shopping trips without stretching the budget. It’s ideal for those who value comfort and stability over top‑end speed.

If you’re comparing this Aventon to other electric cargo bikes, it feels more polished than budget longtails like the Lectric Xpedition 2.0 and Rad Power’s Rad Wagon 5. Yet, the Abound LR costs far less than premium mid‑drive cargo rigs from Tern, Cannondale, and Trek.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it’s one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around. The dual-battery model ($1,799) boasts an incredible 120-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. This makes the XPedition an option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, concessions had to be made somewhere to reach this low price, and the result is a somewhat cheap feel. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but it is erratic at times. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend.

Tern’s Quick Haul Long is enticing because it delivers the core functionality of the pricier GSD series at a lower price. While the Quick Haul Long’s frame isn’t as sleek as the GSD and lacks a suspension fork, the bike still has everything needed to be a true car replacement.

The Quick Haul features include hydraulic disc brakes, a robust double kickstand, a built-in frame lock, trailer attachment points, and an impressive maximum weight limit of 419 pounds. Tern also offers a wide range of accessories to customize the bike to your individual needs. Even when loaded with two kids and a trailer full of groceries, the Bosch Cargo Line motor handles the load with ease. However, don’t expect a speedy ride when fully laden. The bike can handle the load (and you’ll get where you want to go), but it won’t zip to its maximum pedal-assist speed of 20 mph when weighed down.

If you like the look, features, and price of Aventon’s Abound LR but want a smaller package, the SR is the bike for you. The SR has the same 440-pound carrying capacity and 60-mile range as its longtail sibling, but on a shorter wheelbase chassis. This makes it ideal for riders with space constraints (such as apartments and RVs) or anyone seeking a quick ride around town.

The Specialized Globe Haul ST packs 419 pounds of cargo capacity into a surprisingly compact frame. With powerful brakes, dialed geometry, and well-thought-out features, it’s ready for commuting, grocery getting, neighborhood errands, or getting a child to daycare. Without active suspension, the Haul relies on massive 3.5-inch tires for its ride comfort, which work well on all but the roughest roads.

My partner, Julia, purchased a Haul ST after reading the Bike of the Year review. She uses it for commuting in Boston and describes the Haul as zippy. She said, “The power levels are flexible, and I can easily adjust them to how I want to ride or tackle hills.” She also likes the cargo configurations for carrying groceries and running errands. Julia also likes the Haul’s geometry; “It’s nice to ride upright, and it gives me more visibility.”

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

The Fetch+ 4 is Trek’s take on the classic Dutch bakfiets. This bike is essentially the minivan of bikes—it carries up to four kids. It includes two child seats, but you can add accessories to improve your passengers’ comfort. These include a full cover for the basket to keep everyone out of the wind and rain. To power the Fetch, Trek uses Bosch’s BES3 system with a Bosch Cargo Drive motor. It delivers power via a Gates Carbon belt drive for virtually maintenance-free operation.

Most families know Radio Flyer for its iconic red wagons, tricycles, and ride-on toys, but did you know the company also made a range of electric bikes? I use “made” here because, unfortunately, Flyer is backing away from e-bikes to concentrate on its core business. However, if you buy this bike, you’ll still have after-purchase support and the brand will have spare parts available.

The Loop is a 20-inch-wheel mid-tail model equipped with a 750W hub motor (87Nm torque) and can carry up to two children as passengers. Like a good family bike, Flyer loads the Loop with safety features, including a fully enclosed rear wheel, long front fender, turn signals, and four-piston Magura hydraulic disc brakes. Flyer offers the Loop in one universal frame size (fitting riders 4’11” to 6’3”) and four color choices.

Health & Fitness Editor Monique LeBrun tested the Loop with her six-year-old daughter for several months. “I’ve never ridden an e-bike before, so I was a little skeptical about it, but I really enjoy riding the Radio Flyer,” she said. Lebrun notes that “the seat is very comfortable, and I love that it has a low frame so I can easily step on and off the bike.”

The Tern GSD redefines what a car-replacement bike can be. It’s easy to picture running errands on a cargo bike if you live in a city or a town with great cycling infrastructure. However, many people live in suburbs or other areas not exactly designed for bike commuting. The GSD’s Class 3 Bosch pedal-assist motor, massive cargo capacity, and solid battery range make long hauls realistic, even for riders who live miles from town.

Riders from 5 feet to 6’6” can share the same bike, thanks to quick-release adjustments on the seatpost and handlebar. The bar can even rotate forward for tall riders who want extra reach. The bike also features premium touches you won’t find on low-cost cargo bikes—like a suspension fork, Magura 4-piston hydraulic brakes, an integrated lock, and a suspension seatpost. Practical design details make storage and transport surprisingly manageable: the handlebar folds at the headset, the seat drops quickly, and the whole bike can be tipped upright to rest on its rear rack—perfect for tight garage corners. However, be aware that the GSD’s extra weight can make loading it into a vehicle a two-person task.

Do you need to carry absolutely everything and want to do it in style? If so, an Urban Arrow might be right for you.

This front-loader, basket-style cargo bike is designed for families and people carrying large items like multiple kids, large dogs (plural), a Costco run, or a couch—All things people can carry with an Urban Arrow. Thanks to its 75 Nm Bosch Cargo Line motor and 545Wh battery, it has the torque and range to carry you and your stuff up hills and to your destination without breaking a sweat.

Domestic and international cargo bike popularity has exploded in the past decade, says Xtracycles founder and longtail cargo bike pioneer Ross Evans. There are generally four main styles of cargo bikes: longtail, short-tail, front loader, and the bakfiet (a Dutch term that translates to ‘box bike’). You can also find trike varieties for riders needing to transport heavy loads or more than two children.

➡️ Longtail cargo bikes are the most agile and lightweight design. They transport cargo or passengers on an extended tail section behind the rider.

➡️ Short-tail cargo bikes are a variant of longtail bikes, but with a shorter rear extension that makes them more compact and better suited for those tight on space.

➡️ Front loader bikes place the payload in front of the rider, generally on a low-slung platform adaptable to suit many needs.

➡️ Bakfiet-style bikes feature a large basket (typically in front of the rider) for carrying cargo or transporting multiple passengers.

Moving hundreds of pounds on a bike without a motor is great...if you want to get a workout. But most riders and families don’t want that stress or extra work. That’s why we recommend electric motor-equipped cargo bikes. “Electricity and cargo bikes go together like PB&J,” Evans says. E-cargo bikes feature pedal-assist electric motors that can deliver more than 50 miles of range. This makes cargo bikes more accessible to riders who want car-like convenience in a bike-sized package.

However, the tech comes at a price: Electric cargo bikes are pricier than their non-electric counterparts. Unless you live somewhere completely flat, we think an e-cargo bike is the best choice. Electric motors vastly improve a cargo bike’s usability and can save you money in the long run by making it a more effective car substitute.

Once you’ve purchased a cargo bike, you’ll want the right accessories to maximize its utility. Start on the manufacturer’s website: Many brands sell panniers, racks, and child seats to match their cargo bikes. Alternatively, if your style is more “dump it and go,” bakfiets use a single spacious box—typically upfront—that’ll fit all your stuff (there are still seat belts for your kids). The best way to determine which style or bike you prefer is to take bikes for test rides.

Approach an e-cargo bike and accessory purchase the same way you would if buying a car. Try and test as many options as possible. Prioritize your most common cargo needs. While it can be fun to think in aspirational terms, a bike suited to your daily needs means you use it more often.

These bikes are thoroughly put through their paces by the Bicycling test team. We don’t only test them—we live with them. We haul groceries, drop kids off at school, and squeeze in as many rides as possible to see if these e-cargo bikes can truly replace our cars for daily life. Test Editor Dan Chabanov puts them through the ultimate car-replacement experiment on the streets of his hometown of Philadelphia, and Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy tests them on her daily commute to the office. A

t our Easton, Pennsylvania headquarters, the rest of the team gives these bikes a daily beating, using them to run errands around town (because let’s be honest—e-cargo bikes are just plain fun to ride). We also speak with the product managers behind the designs to understand their choices, and compare each model to its closest competitors to see how they stack up. Bottom line: we test these bikes like we’d use them in real life—because we actually did.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

On Episode 307 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev and Jose Raymond, and the panel compared the current era of competitive bodybuilders with those of the 90s. How would they stack up?

The 90’s was a decade where size dominated the stage. Often referred to as the “Mass Monster” era, stars like Dorian Yates, Lee Haney, and Ronnie Coleman reigned supreme. But how do current muscle men stack up against these icons of the past? Jose Raymond speculated that there may be a drop in quality in the 2020s, because IFBB Pro Cards are too easily won these days. “If you have to fight for a pro card, for seven to ten years, by the time you get it you’ll be ready,” said the bodybuilder-turned-coach. “And the physique is going to be already matured and marinated.”

Raymond felt that younger bodybuilder’s winning pro cards effects the overall talent pool. “The physique isn’t ready,” he said. “Most of today’s guys would not win a pro card in 1993, 1989.”

Agreeing with Raymond’s take, host Dennis James said that “90% of them, maybe even more than 90%,” would not win a pro card if competing in the ’90s. “You’ve got guys getting a pro card for second place,” added Raymond. “That’s crazy to me.”

To further cement this observation, Milos Sarcev explained that respected and revered bodybuilders of the past like Edgar Fletcher and Matt Mendenhall never even turned pro. “Edgar Fletcher would win pro shows today,” said Raymond. “One hundred percent,” agreed Sarcev.

The Menace further explained that there have been more than 70 athletes qualifying for Olympia categories, from a pool of around 500, although this is being tightened up in many divisions with the requirement to win two shows. So, perhaps restoring quality over quantity is the key to creating the best era.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding news and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.

#8859. Barbell Grip Guide: How Hand Placement Optimizes Bench, Press, and Squat Form

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Grip sets the table for what comes next because where you place your hands affects wrist position, elbow path, shoulder comfort, stability, and often good form.

Your arm length, shoulder and wrist mobility, and training goal can all influence your grip. Grip is essential for rows, deadlifts, and curl variations, but for presses and squats we often ignore it.

However, paying special attention to it will pay dividends. The goal is to find a grip that makes the lift feel comfortable, strong, and minimizes discomfort.

Here, we’ll break down the best hand positions for the barbell bench press, overhead press, back squat, and front squat, including the grip options for each and how to decide which one fits you best.

We often only think about grip when it fails, but taking the time to set it often makes the difference between a good set and a bad one.

Let’s begin here. Your bench press grip affects wrist position, elbow path, range of motion, shoulder stress, and which muscles work hardest.

Where the Bar Should Sit: Start by placing the bar toward the heels of your palms. This keeps the bar stacked over your forearm and helps prevent wrist hyperextension. Think of your hand, wrist, and forearm as a unit. The better your forearm and wrist stack, the better your bench press.

Grip Width: Begin with your pinky finger wrapped around the barbell ring. This grip is the best starting point for most lifters. At the bottom of the rep, your forearms should be nearly vertical.

A wider grip shortens the range of motion and emphasizes the pecs, but it also moves the shoulder into greater abduction. That can feel strong for some but cranky for others.

A narrower grip increases range of motion and puts more demand on the triceps because the elbows stay closer to the torso and get a deeper stretch. Neither one is better or worse. It depends on comfort and your training goal.

Full Grip vs. False Grip: A full grip, with the thumb wrapped around the bar, gives you the best bar security and should be your default. However, a false grip (without the thumb) may provide more comfort for some lifters, but the tradeoff is less bar security.

How to Know Which Grip Is Best for You: Use the grip and choose the grip width that best balances shoulder comfort, wrist alignment, and stability.

Bar placement and grip width are vital for the barbell overhead press. Maintaining the wrist, forearm, and elbow stack will help you press with power without driving your upper-body joints mad.

Where the Bar Should Sit: The bar should sit toward the heel of the palm, not near the fingers. This places the load over the forearm and helps prevent wrist hyperextension, but some wrist extension in the OH press is normal. The goal is not to force the wrist straight, but to avoid letting the bar roll so far back that it becomes uncomfortable.

Grip Width: For most lifters, a grip just outside shoulder width is a good place to start. If it’s too wide, you shorten the range of motion and may lose leverage. If it’s too narrow, your elbows and shoulders can feel crowded at the bottom. From the front, your forearms should be close to vertical, with the elbows slightly in front of the bar.

Full Grip vs. False Grip: A full grip gives you the most security and should be the default for most lifters. A false grip can feel better for some people because it may reduce wrist bend. The tradeoff, again, is less bar security.

How to Know Which Grip Is Best for You: Use the grip that lets you start with a solid wrist position, keep the forearms vertical, and press without shoulder or elbow irritation.

Grip is secondary to the squat, but your hands secure the bar and help create upper-back tension while your back supports the load.

Use a False Grip: For the back squat, I prefer a false or thumbless grip, with the thumb resting on the same side of the bar as the fingers.

Why? It makes it easier to keep the wrist in line with the forearm instead of letting the wrist bend back under the bar. This helps prevent your hands from taking the load that should be on your back.

Grip Width: A narrower grip can increase upper-back tension by pulling the shoulder blades together and locking the bar in place. But narrower isn’t always better.

If you don’t have the shoulder mobility to reach that position, forcing your hands too close can irritate your wrists, elbows, or shoulders. Moving the hands slightly wider often gives you enough room to keep the wrists aligned while keeping the upper back tight.

How to Know Which Grip Width Is Best for You: Use the narrowest grip you can comfortably maintain while keeping:

If you’re getting wrist or inner-elbow soreness before you squat, widening the hands a little is the better solution.

The front squat gives you more grip options than the back squat because grip is secondary. The goal is to have the bar resting securely across the front of your shoulders while your hands support it.

There are three practical ways to do that.

The best front-squat grip keeps the bar secure, your elbows high, and your torso upright without causing unnecessary discomfort. There’s no need to force-feed one grip when you have options.

Here are the key points to pay attention to with barbell squats and presses.

Does it improve joint alignment? Your wrists, elbows, and shoulders should feel natural and not engaged in a game of Twister.

Does it reduce pain or irritation? A grip that bothers your wrists, elbows, or shoulders is worth changing. Adjust your grip width, switch from a full grip to a false grip, or try a different front-squat setup to fix it.

Are you stronger with it? If one grip gives you better control and lets you get after it without sacrificing technique, then go with that.

Can you maintain the intended range of motion? If your grip shortens your range of motion or forces you into bad lifting positions, it probably needs adjusting.

The key is to make small changes and judge them by how the whole lift feels and performs. A good grip should increase stability and express strength, not add another thing to fight against.

Your grip should make the lift better, not give you another problem to solve.

Paying attention to joint alignment and discomfort before you lift puts you in the best position to succeed. So don’t be afraid to adjust if you’ve been told to grip a certain way; a small grip change can improve comfort, stability, and strength more than most lifters expect.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#8855. Anita Herbert Shares Her Upper-Body Smith Machine Workout

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There’s nothing quite like lifting a barbell loaded with weighted plates when you are looking to dial in your resistance training efforts, but for many people, the idea of balancing a free weight seems daunting, and for others, mobility issues or a lack of experience can become a serious obstacle. It’s good to know then, that buff beauty Anita Herbert has sculpted herself into phenomenal shape by including the Smith machine into her rotation.

“Here are some of my favorite back and shoulder exercises you can add to your next upper body session, using just a Smith machine,” offered the Hungarian in a recent Instagram post for her “Fit Queen Army” on Instagram. This fit female is not only a transformative coach, but she is also an IFBB Pro. “Save this for your next upper body day!” Herbert advised her 150,000-plus followers.

The “FitQueen” showed how to get the most from each machine

Machines, just like free weights, can build muscle by progressive overload, and this session is stacked with plenty of heavy reps. Aim for 8 to 12 on each exercise to put your body into a state of hypertrophy, forcing to adaptations that will build your muscles back stronger.

For her first superset, the Fit Queen begins with the shoulder press, primarily working her anterior deltoid at the front of the shoulder, and also recruiting the upper back, triceps, and core. Next, using a supinated grip, comes the inverted row for taxing the mid-back, lats, and rear delts.

The second superset calls for a pullup that is great for athletes of any level, because you will raise your body from a seated position, and can use the feet for further stabilization. Using a wide grip, pause for a short time at the top of the lift, in order to increase time under tension. This will work the lats, rhomboids, and upper trapezius, but be sure not to shrug, and concentrate on a smooth range of motion. This exercise is followed by the single arm shoulder press, to fix any strength imbalances and fire up those front deltoids once again.

The third and final superset starts with a single-arm row, hitting the lats, traps, and rear delts, while also activating the rotator cuff and forearms. Keep your core braced and focus on engaging the back, while keeping the elbows close to the body. The last move is the upright row for building some serious boulder shoulders. You will also work the triceps and upper back as you improve grip strength all at the same time.

While it is true that the Smith machine stabilizes the weight and reduces the chance of injury, you may be surprised to find that the load can feel heavier on this device.

“It can feel heavier than free weights, especially for upper body exercises because Smith machines have different bar weights, counterbalance systems and resistance,” explained Herbert, who provided further advice to her seriously impressed followers in the comments section. “The fixed bar path also changed how the movement feels, compared to free weights.”

#8848. How ‘Agent of Shadows’ Star Chase Mattson Packed on Nearly 30 Pounds of Lean Muscle

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Model and actor Chase Mattson has become one of vertical media’s most sought after actors, so when the star was asked to chop it up with the superstars of WWE for ReelShort’s Agent of Shadows, he went all-in, gaining respect for these larger-than-life talents in the process, and telling M&F that he prepares himself for any challenge through serious training and a dedicated attitude to nutrition.

In today’s world, vertical media makes sense. As younger people shun the traditional television and scroll away on social media, the premise of shooting shows vertically allows for seamless viewing on phones. Still, with vertical micro-dramas offering free episodes before a pay wall hides the ending, the pressure to perform to the best of his abilities, for every second, is not lost on Chase Mattson, who was recently named People magazine’s Sexiest ReelShort Star. He’s also become one of the genre’s most able actors.

Mattson’s latest project is titled Agent of Shadows, and is a collaboration between ReelShort and WWE, featuring grapplers such as Drew McIntyre, Booker T, Jacob Fatu, and Nikkita Lyons. And, while Mattson, himself was a highly active athlete in his youth, the 6’3” star was in awe of the likes of McIntyre, who is 6’5.” “I was told that Drew was a big guy and I was like, ‘okay cool, I’m a big guy,’ and then he came on set and this dude is a giant, man!” Fortunately, the star says that he and McIntyre became fast friends.”

Among Mattson’s preferred workouts is the “Cindy” workout, a CrossFit circuit that  Tom Holland has employed to stay in Spider-Man shape. To try it, you’ll perform 5 pullups, 10 pushups, and 15 air squats, then repeat for as many rounds as you can. “I was like, that seems too easy but the first time, I got to round eight, and I was gassed,” shares Mattson. Now, the actor has reached a peak of 16 rounds and is even pushing himself further by squatting with 40-pound dumbbells.

With four kids (and two dogs), Mattson balances family life by embracing the chaos, but with the actor eating five meals per day, you better not touch his bison! Mattson explains that as a model, he simply wasn’t eating enough, but after seeking advice on nutrition, he now tracks his macros, and that means carbs are back in. The star explains that at home, he has his own cupboard for food, meaning that he can stick to his plan in order to stay screen ready.

“We have cabinets in our house, but I have one that us dedicated just for me,” explains Mattson of how he is able to stay focused and avoid the sweet temptations that may be lurking in other areas of the kitchen. The star makes smart swaps, like almonds instead of candy, and eats a large number of blueberries for the effects on muscle recovery. His commitment has certainly paid off, and the actor now weighs in at a lean and muscular 215 pounds as opposed to the 185-pound frame from his modeling days.

Still, when it comes to working out, Mattson often makes it a family affair and shares the fun side of fitness with outdoor jogs and calisthenics, which are great for young bodies.

Not only does he have to stay ripped for the next project, and that could mean just 24-hours’ notice for a shirtless scene, but during the shoot for Agent of Shadows, things got seriously physical. One scene even called for Mattson to mix it up with WWE Hall of Famer Booker T, while filming in the blazing heat of the desert.

“Physically, I was doing all the WWE stunts on the ground,” he explains, noting that his whole body was sore “for days” afterwards.

Mattson went above and beyond with the promotion of this vertical micro-drama too, enrolling at WWE’s Performance Center and stepping inside the ring for real.

“They hit me with a chair, a real chair,” says the actor, reflecting on the surreal nature of his job. “It’s harder than it looks.”

With all of the major streaming platforms now developing, or already offering vertical media, Mattson finds himself as one of the most experienced performers in this area, but as we conclude our conversation, the much sought after star is readying for a flight that will see him working on a regular, horizontal project. Still, in true secret agent style, he can’t tell us anything about it.

“I always stay ready, so I don’t have to get ready,” he signs off.
