#8835. The Best Whey Protein Powders of 2025, According to a Certified Sports Nutrition Coach

Whey protein powders are a convenient way to up your daily protein intake. We tested over 50 to choose the best whey protein on the market.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Whey protein powder is a popular supplement because it’s a simple and effective way to increase daily protein intake.

Whey is a complete protein that contains all nine essential amino acids our bodies need to build muscle. Whey protein also supplies the body with branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), like leucine, which help promote muscle growth (1).

We consulted Pete Nastasi, a certified nutrition coach (C.N.C.), to help us find the best whey protein powders on the market.

Here, we break down the different types of whey protein powders available (concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate), which types will work best for you, and what nutrition information to look for. Plus, we’ve tested over 50 protein powders to help us create the list of our top picks.

Medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

We chose products for our list of the best whey protein powders based on a number of factors reflected in our whey protein powder scoring methodology. These include:

We also receive input from our panel of expert contributors, which includes registered dietitians and highly credentialed experts in sports nutrition and exercise science.

No sugar, all protein—that’s what Transparent Labs set out to accomplish with its grass-fed whey protein isolate. This whey protein undergoes filtration (2), taking out the excess sugar, fat, carbs, and lactose so you’re giving your body the pure protein it needs to rebuild. Whey isolate has the highest protein concentration of the different types of protein powders, and this protein is a good option if you’re trying to reduce your carb and fat intake.

Transparent Labs’ Whey Protein Isolate packs 28 grams of protein into each serving—one of the highest on our list. We also like the flavor variety, including unique flavors like Cinnamon French Toast. Bonus: This protein isn’t too sweet, so you can mix it with fruit juice or add it to a fruit smoothie without feeling like you’re drinking a shake made with Fun Dip.

Sports Research Whey Protein is formulated with 6.9 grams of BCAAs, including 1,000 milligrams of L-leucine. Studies show leucine may help reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Depending on flavor, this Informed Sport Certified protein powder is sweetened with stevia or sucralose, so those sensitive to these ingredients may need to steer clear.

Rachel Pasche says she has a protein shake for dessert some nights using the Dutch Chocolate flavor. “It might be too sweet for some people, but I honestly love the taste so much,” she says. “It’s my favorite flavor of protein powder I’ve ever tried.” She says the powder mixes well with water alone, with both a handheld mixer and in a shaker cup, noting there is some foam at the top that doesn’t last long and no clumping.

Additionally, Pasche says she sometimes feels bloated after whey protein shakes, but after six months of using Sports Research Whey, she has not experienced any bloat.

Why is grass-fed whey protein better? Studies show that dairy sourced from grass-fed cows has a higher concentration of whey proteins and amino acids (3), which may further support muscular training adaptations.

This Nutricost protein powder is non-GMO, gluten-free, and third-party tested. Whey protein concentrate, like this one, is often made with sunflower lecithin, an ingredient to help promote mixability. Testers also enjoy the taste and say this protein powder mixes well. “The taste was nostalgic; I’d liken it to Nesquik,” says tester Grant Smith. “And the mixability was on par with some of the better proteins I’ve had previously.” Smith was pleasantly surprised by the mixability of Nutricost Whey Protein, noting he didn’t find any small chunks of undissolved protein floating in his shake when mixed with milk.

After drinking most of his shake, Smith let a bit of the mixture sit for almost 10 minutes after initially mixing to test for separation. He noticed some slight separation between the protein and skim milk he mixed it with, but says it wasn’t enough to make the drink any less appealing.

The protein in Legion Athletics is certified to contain no banned substances by Labdoor, the gold standard of third-party lab testing. This helps ensure the protein isolate is in its purest, most nutritionally dense form without any interference from pesticides and growth hormones.

Additionally, Legion Athletics whey is filtered to remove extra carbs and fat, so you’re only getting the good stuff with every serving. The removal of these elements is geared toward bloat-free digestion.

Testers say it also tastes great, giving especially high marks to the French Vanilla flavor. “I really like the flavor of this one. It tastes like a vanilla creamer!” says Kayla Godfrey. “This is delicious. Great vanilla taste,” says Carlo Barajas.

You’ve probably seen that one of the biggest general complaints about protein powder is it can taste “chalky” and leave you with an off-putting aftertaste. Our testing team tried Gainful’s Caffe Mocha flavor, and liked the subtle, not-too-sweet flavor profile. “This reminds me of an at-home cappuccino mix,” says Barry Bridges. “The coffee flavor is very light—I’d say it’s more of a chocolate flavor,” adds Rachael Harris.

If you’re not a fan of coffee flavors, Gainful offers nine total flavors in individual-use packets, so you can pick and choose what you’re craving each day. Nastasi, who has tried many different Gainful Protein Powder flavors, says the Chocolate Peanut Butter, Caffe Mocha, and Sea Salt Caramel are his favorites.

Whey protein is a concentrated protein source derived from cow’s milk, which contains two major proteins called casein and whey (4). Whey accounts for 20 percent of milk protein, and is considered a high-quality protein source. Cow’s milk protein is considered a complete protein because it contains all nine essential amino acids required by the body (5).

Beyond basic nutrition, whey protein (6) may offer specific health benefits, such as enhanced immune function (7) and cardiometabolic health (8). Usually, whey is sold in powder form, which can be blended with water or other liquids or added to soft foods. Also, people use whey protein powder in cooking, which adds nutritional value to baked goods. Food manufacturers use whey formulations rather than cream, butter, or egg ingredients to make high-protein, low-fat products.

When you browse online or at your local nutrition shop for whey protein products, you’ll probably notice different forms of whey. The main difference in the types of whey protein is how they’re processed. The three most common forms of whey protein are concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate (hydrolyzed whey).

Whey protein concentrate (WPC) is the least processed form of whey, so it contains the highest levels of lactose (milk sugar), fat, carbohydrates, and nutrients. Food manufacturers use WPC (9) to replace fresh dairy and eggs in products like sauces, soups, and baked goods because it adds flavor, color, and texture and extends shelf-life (10). However, it has the lowest protein content out of the three—typically 70 to 80 percent.

Whey protein isolate (WPI) is made when whey is filtered and processed. It contains the most protein, 90 percent or more, and less lactose. Because of its higher protein content, sports nutrition companies often prefer WPI for use in supplements, protein bars, and other protein products (11). However, it lacks some of the beneficial nutrients found in the concentrated form (12).

Whey protein hydrolysate (WPH), also known as hydrolyzed whey, is produced by a process called partial hydrolysis, which breaks down whey protein for easier absorption (13). WPH is digested faster than WPC or WPI (14), so it causes a 28 to 43 percent increase in blood sugar levels (15). Diabetics don’t have to worry about this, though. Protein digestion is slow. In fact, recent research suggests that whey protein improves glycemic (blood sugar) control (16).

The real benefit of a whey protein powder is that it’s an incredibly convenient and high-quality source of dietary protein. However, if you consume enough dietary protein through meat, dairy, legumes, and other foods, then you don’t need a protein powder to achieve your health and fitness goals. However, if you’re having trouble consuming enough protein through your diet alone, then adding a protein powder to your daily routine can have some real benefits.

Whey protein is rich in essential amino acids, including BCAAs, which can be beneficial for supporting muscle integrity and growth with training (17). Adding a protein powder for muscle gain to your daily diet can be a great way to help maximize your dietary protein intake and stimulate muscle growth.

When you’re in a caloric deficit with the goal of losing weight, you want to ensure that the weight you’re losing is primarily fat and not muscle. Eating a diet rich in protein helps preserve the lean muscle mass you’ve worked hard to achieve and enables your body to prioritize burning fat for energy.

Consuming whey protein has a satiating effect, meaning that it helps you feel full for a longer period of time. High protein diets help with weight loss by regulating your hunger levels and therefore reducing the amount of total calories you consume throughout the day.

In order to properly use a whey protein powder, you should first determine how much protein you should be eating on a daily basis. The amount of protein you consume is dependent on your fitness goals and current body weight, activity level, and physique. A simple way to calculate your daily protein intake is by multiplying your body weight by 0.8. The resulting number is how many grams of protein you should consume each day. This should provide most active individuals with sufficient protein intake. Remember that whey protein powder is a supplement and shouldn’t be your main source of dietary protein.

As far as how to consume this protein powder, you should follow the instructions on the supplement label. This usually entails mixing one scoop of protein powder with 10 to 12 ounces of your favorite beverage. It can also be mixed in a smoothie or foods like oatmeal and pancake batter. Whey protein powder can be consumed at any time of the day, but it’s usually utilized as a post-workout supplement to begin repairing muscle tissue.

When used in moderation, protein powder is free of side effects and generally considered safe for healthy adults. However, consuming large amounts of protein powder can lead to digestive issues, dehydration, and (potentially) nutrient deficiencies. It’s important to use whey protein powder as part of a balanced diet and not as your main source of dietary protein. If you experience any unusual symptoms after using protein powder, stop use immediately and consult a healthcare professional.

A whey protein powder will benefit anyone who is looking to increase their daily protein consumption and has trouble doing so through their diet alone. This is especially relevant for very active individuals, such as athletes, bodybuilders, and fitness enthusiasts who have increased protein demands due to their workouts and training.

Another segment of the population that may benefit from using a whey protein powder is older adults. As we age, our bodies become less efficient at absorbing protein from food (18). Using protein supplements can be an easy way for older adults to meet their daily protein needs and support muscle health.

When picking a whey protein product, there are a few factors to consider, including the type of protein, taste, nutrition, additives/allergies, and price.

Check the ingredients list to see what type of whey the protein powder contains. Some brands will use a blend of whey forms.

Whey proteins come in a wide variety of flavors. You’ll find options from unflavored to vanilla, chocolate orange, and summer berries, to name a few. Taste is important because you want a protein supplement you’ll enjoy. When just starting to supplement your protein intake, try a small container or buy samples of flavors you might enjoy and get creative with your add-ins. You can try fruits, flavored milks, or juices to create new flavors that fit your taste preference.

Check the whey protein label for the amount of protein per serving, and factor it into your daily protein intake. Most protein powders have around 25 grams per serving, which is an ideal dosage to maximize muscle protein synthesis (19). Also look for calories, fats, carbs, fiber, vitamins, and minerals and even amino acid profiles. Make sure that the supplement you choose gives you the maximum benefit without unnecessary add-ins.

Read the ingredients section, too. Look for additives or allergens that you want or need to avoid. For example, labels warn you if the whey powder contains soy or was processed in a facility with nuts.

The protein powders on our list give you a good idea of the price range for whey supplements. Our top picks vary from $1.16 to $3.41 per serving or $34 to $95 per container, so there’s an option for most budgets.

It depends on your body’s unique needs and health and fitness goals. You should include protein with meals or snacks every three to five hours (20), but no one should rely solely on protein powder because that would eliminate other nutritious whole foods from the diet.One whey protein drink per day is reasonable. Check with your doctor if you want to use whey protein to replace more than one meal.

Yes, whey protein powder is generally considered safe for healthy individuals when used in moderation. If you have any pre-existing medical conditions or have a severe lactose intolerance, consult with a healthcare professional before adding a whey protein powder to your diet.

There really is no “best time” to take a whey protein powder supplement. Instead, your timing depends on your individual goals and lifestyle. Some people enjoy a protein shake in the morning as a quick and easy breakfast option they can have on the go, while others prefer to consume it immediately after a workout to support muscle growth and recovery.Just remember that whey protein powder should be used as a supplement to a well-balanced diet, and should not be used as a replacement for whole nutrient-dense foods. The timing of when you consume the whey protein is less important than your overall protein intake throughout the day.

From keeping you satiated to helping you improve your performance in the gym, whey protein powder can certainly help you lose weight. Research has even shown that whey protein may reduce abdominal fat when combined with weight training (21).

If overused, whey protein can cause side effects (22), including kidney or liver damage, aggression, acne, and a disruption in gut bacteria. Since most people don’t consume more than one serving of whey protein per day, overconsumption is rare and takes time to develop. If you would like to add an extra layer of protection for your gut bacteria, you can even take a high-quality prebiotic or ensure you consume a variety of fruits and vegetables on a regular basis.

The best way to know if your whey protein is high quality is to read the labels. Check out the whey source, nutritional profile, and ingredient list. Quality wheys use traceable, organic, and certified ingredients. Also, high-quality whey products avoid fillers and artificial sweeteners. Another sign that you have a good quality whey is when the labels include certifications and seals from third-party approvals. These show that the manufacturer has proven the quality by established standards.

Stephen is an ISSA-certified personal trainer and nutritionist with an immense passion for health and fitness. A two-time University of Florida graduate and longtime rugby player, he brings more than a decade of strength training experience, plus a diverse writing and editing background. When he’s not creating content or hitting the gym, he enjoys traveling, cooking, and attending music festivals around the world.

The Breaking Muscle newsletter is everything you need to know about strength in a 3 minute read.

Breaking Muscle is the fitness world’s preeminent destination for timely, high-quality information on exercise, fitness, health, and nutrition. Our audience encompasses the entire spectrum of the fitness community: consumers, aficionados, fitness professionals, and business owners. We seek to inform, educate and advocate for this community.

#8834. Julius Thomas Speaks His Mind When It Comes to Peak Performance

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

When Julius Thomas hung up his NFL cleats in 2018, he didn’t know he was about to face the hardest, and longest, transition of his life. The tight end who caught touchdowns from Peyton Manning walked into graduate school at 30 with no job, no playbook, and none of the daily wins football used to hand him.

“When you have to go from a master to a rookie, you go from winning a lot, knowing what you’re doing and very comfortable with all of it, to then having to rebuild that,” he recalled. “That is extremely challenging, because in the beginning of any journey, it’s losing, doing it wrong, working really hard, struggling through it.”

The lessons he learned over the years that followed changed the way he looked at performance. He went back to the classroom, completed a clinical residency and earned his doctorate in clinical psychology in June 2025.

In pro sports, the mentality is often to push through and keep going. While Thomas lived that for years, today, as a performance coach and consultant with his company Optimal Performance, he sees how much of peak performance relies on stepping back and checking in with ourselves.

“One of the things I say is the biggest unaddressed area of performance in all of sport is emotional regulation,” Thomas told Muscle & Fitness.

The 2026 NFL season has already tested the push-through mindset from the opening weeks. Six of the 32 quarterbacks initially named starters were hurt early in the season, including Jayden Daniels, Caleb Williams and Jaxson Dart. Now Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is now expected to miss the rest of the season after doctors found deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, with his case traced back to a calf injury from an opponent’s cleat.

Thomas resisted pinning the run on any single cause. He also didn’t think any of this was unusual. “Football has a 100% injury rate” he says. “Every single person that plays football is going to get injured, so injuries are just high in that sport in general.”

Contact injuries come with the job, he said, while training loads, surfaces, off-season habits, mobility, and recovery—or the lack thereof—shape the non-contact ones. Research has also shown that the mind does have a seat at the table.

A 2017 meta-analysis in Sports Medicine linked stress responses to higher injury risk and found psychological interventions reduced injury rates. Hence, Thomas makes it a point to take our foot off the gas a lot more frequently than we do.

“If you just only floor it, only floor it, only floor it. How long do you think that engine is going to do well?” Thomas explains. “Not very long.”

The brakes represent the parasympathetic nervous system, the rest-and-digest branch that counters the stress response. “If we don’t do enough to create more parasympathetic tone in our nervous system, if we don’t sleep enough hours, all we’re doing is degrading the major systems in our body,” he explained, noting the cost of the grind will come sooner or later.

This pattern follows high performers into the boardroom as well. Thomas has coached executives who asked him for nootropics to sharpen their focus—then admitted that he himself was only getting four hours of sleep a night for 20 years. So he’s built a framework called “Striving for 100” to bring clients back to five daily habits, including exercise, sleep, nutrition, recovery and healthy substance use, with recovery anchoring the rest. One-on-one, he layers in radical acceptance, cognitive restructuring and reframing drawn from several evidence-based methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT).

“You’re either gonna pay the cost slowly and surely by recovering in your 30s and 40s and 50s,” he says, “or you’re gonna pay it all of a sudden when you’re sick.”

He holds himself to the same standard. Though when a friend had warned him a full transition would take about a decade, he refused to believe it.

“I am eight years in transition. And I’m almost to where I want to be in my next profession,” he admitted, but pointed out the difficulty he’s experienced with identity and how much our society gets it wrong.

Thomas bristles at the advice athletes often hear on the way out, that they simply need to separate who they are from the sport they played.

“It really bothers me when people say that about athletes, because they’re trying to minimize the challenge of the experience, so that when the athlete finds himself in the psychological challenge, they feel like they shouldn’t be, and this should be easy,” he explained, adding that identity runs deeper than a label, and it’s built by what you do every day and reinforced by how others see you.

Years after his last game, people still want to talk about NFL playing days, in which the two-time Pro Bowl tight end caught 12 touchdown passes in both 2012 and 2013. “It’s hard to get people to see you in your new career,” he admitted.

Now he prepares athletes for that shift and asks them whether they’re ready for one of the hardest things they’ll ever do, and whether they’ve built the tools to get through it.

“Do you have the psychological skills to reframe, recontextualize, find meaning, find purpose?” he’d ask.

What he doesn’t want any player to forget is that the struggle says nothing about them. Every major life change strains us. “Transitions are always hard,” he said. But with the right tools and support, it becomes easier to navigate over time.

Most of us were never taught to name what we feel, let alone work through it when stress drags on for months. Thomas wasn’t either, and he’s seen the toll it could take on the body.

“Emotions trigger our nervous system,” he says, referring to his studies in psychoneuroimmunology. “So the better you get at managing emotions and reducing negative emotions, the less sustained stress you’d have on your nervous system.”

And it matters because our nervous system, immune system, and psychology are connected, he says, and when stress becomes chronic, various aspects of our life take a hit. Sleep and diet slip first when emotional strain builds, he noted, and muscle tension climbs as anxiety lingers.

However, simply putting a feeling into words can help turn the volume down. A 2007 UCLA brain imaging study in Psychological Science found that labeling emotions dampened the amygdala’s response to negative images.

Though few of us get support doing that work. He cited CDC data that reported 10.9% of U.S. men receive counseling or therapy from a mental health professional, compared with 16.9% of women. And, unfortunately, Thomas sees where we choose to spend time and money instead.

“People are not interested in paying for mental health services, but they’re really interested in new pants and new shirts and nice bags,” he said, adding how much easier it is for many of us to ask for help with physical pain or discomfort. As a player, he never hesitated to walk into the training room with a sore ankle.

“We are constantly asking for help in so many areas of our life,” he says, “but we somehow, as a culture, believe that we should handle what’s in our heart and in our mind by ourselves.”

Certainly, Thomas is no rookie in his new career, and it shows in the company he keeps. At Eudēmonia on November 5-8, he will share the stage with some of the movers and shakers of the health, wellness and longevity industry.

He recalled his first year at the event and how much the relationships he built across psychology, neuroscience, medicine and mind-body practices have stayed with him.

“The conversations, the network, the community I built at year one at Eudēmonia is still having positive influence on my life almost one year later,” he said. “And Eudēmonia has become one of the conferences that I’m most excited to go to.”

Thomas returns with keynotes on mental health and a panel discussion on mindset, performance and the capacity to adapt. The takeaway he wants the audience to leave with is hope, actionable steps, and to be educated in something that is going to help make them healthier, better, more productive and higher functioning.

“If you want sustainable high performance, you have to build well-being and quality of life into what you do,” he said.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Avios are accessible from virtually every major transferable points currency:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Go to ba.com, log into your Executive Club account, and complete the award booking. You'll pay the Avios balance plus applicable government taxes and fees (typically $5–$30 for Aer Lingus partner bookings — far less than BA's own flight surcharges). Enter passenger details, select seats, and confirm.

Aer Lingus joined the Oneworld alliance, which means British Airways Avios can book Aer Lingus-operated flights. Because BA uses distance-based pricing, the relatively short transatlantic crossing from the East Coast to Dublin (roughly 3,000-3,500 miles) prices at just 13,000 Avios each way in economy. Compare this to using American Airlines miles (30,000+ each way) or other programs for the same transatlantic flight. The distance-based chart rewards this specific geography with disproportionately low pricing, creating one of the best-value transatlantic sweet spots available.

Verify that Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from your departure city to Dublin. The strongest year-round service is from Boston and New York. Seasonal routes may only operate during summer months.

Log into your British Airways Executive Club account and search for flights from your city to Dublin using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for Aer Lingus-operated flights (flight numbers starting with EI). Check flexible dates for the best availability.

Once you find availability, transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant from Chase and Amex.

Complete the booking on ba.com. The total will show 13,000 Avios plus taxes and surcharges (typically $50-$100 each way). Review the total out-of-pocket before confirming to make sure it meets your value threshold.

Add your Aer Lingus or Oneworld frequent flyer number to earn status credits. Remember that Dublin offers U.S. Preclearance for return flights — a significant time-saver. Consider booking accommodations using hotel points for a fully points-funded trip.

Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from Boston (BOS), New York (JFK), Newark (EWR), Hartford (BDL), Philadelphia (PHL), Washington Dulles (IAD), Chicago (ORD), and other seasonal routes. Boston and New York have the most frequent service year-round.

Aer Lingus awards do carry fuel surcharges, typically $100-$200 round trip in economy. While not zero, this is still dramatically less than the $500-$1,000+ cash fare. The net savings remain substantial despite the surcharges.

Dublin can serve as an excellent gateway to the rest of Europe. Aer Lingus offers connections to many European cities from Dublin, and you can also book separate budget airline flights within Europe. Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: New members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

The BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.
